And what constitutes the root of the afflictions (kleśa)?
This refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, including false and erroneous views, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals.
Furthermore, that which is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) should be understood as being subsumed by these [defilements] and as the sprout of suffering that is produced thereby.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom, compassion, and other qualities are able to sever those sprouts; for this reason, the analogy of a sword is employed.
As the verse says:
"Because the Buddha can grasp the sword of wisdom and compassion, he cuts away all sprouts of suffering."
Furthermore, the afflictions subsumed under wrong views and doubt are abandoned through the Path of Seeing;
they cannot be known by worldly wisdom, nor can they be destroyed by the dense forest of afflictions, just as one cannot destroy forests, walls, and the like within the world.
Those similar dharmas can be destroyed by the power of the Tathāgata; for this reason, the simile of the vajra-pestle is taught.
The verse says:
"And because of the sublime vajra-pestle, it shatters the mountains of all views, as well as the concealed, inverted minds and all dense thickets."

These six kinds of phrases are explained in sequence within the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* (*Rulai zhuangyan zhihui guangming ru yiqie fo jingjie jing*); they should be understood accordingly.
How should this be understood?
That sutra states: "Mañjuśrī!"
That the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither born nor extinguished clarifies the unconditioned nature of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, it is further explained through nine similes, beginning with the manifestation of the reflected image of the body of Śakra, King of Devas, within a stainless and pure ground of lapis lazuli, all of which clarify that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished.

Furthermore, it is said: "Mañjuśrī! The pure *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise thus: it is unmoving and unarisen; the mind does not engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is without discrimination, non-discriminating, and free from the act of discriminating; it is without thought, without thinking, and inconceivable; it is without recollection, quiescent, and tranquil; it is neither born nor extinguished; it cannot be seen or heard, cannot be smelled or tasted, cannot be touched, and is devoid of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*); it cannot be perceived and cannot be known."
These and other such phrases all describe the various characteristics of tranquility.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that within all the Buddha’s activities, he is free from all conceptual proliferation and discrimination, being tranquil and spontaneous.
Next, the remaining sūtras are explained.
Among them, it is said: "One who realizes all dharma-gates as they truly are. This clarifies that the Tathāgata, by not relying on others, has realized great bodhi.
Furthermore, it is further stated that the Tathāgata’s bodhi consists of sixteen kinds; therefore, the sūtra says: "Mañjuśrī!

The Tathāgata thus awakens to all phenomena as they truly are, and observing the impurity, defilement, and blemish of the *dharmatā* of all sentient beings, he manifests great compassion toward them with vigorous power."
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom and compassion should be understood as follows: Mañjuśrī,
when the Tathāgata thus awakens to all phenomena as they truly are, he realizes, as previously explained, that their essence is to have no essence.
"Awakening to reality as it is" means knowing through the non-conceptual Buddha-wisdom exactly as it is.

"Observing the *dharmatā* of all sentient beings" means that even for those in the category of the "wrongly disposed," their *dharmatā*, *dharmakāya*, *dharmadhātu*, and *tathāgatagarbha* are no different from those within my own body; this is because the Tathāgata’s wisdom-eye perceives them with complete clarity.
It is "impure" because ordinary worldlings possess the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
It is "stained" because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others possess the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
"Having some" refers to the fact that various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others rely on those two kinds of habitual tendencies as obstacles.

"Mastery" (vaiśāradya) refers to the ability to know, according to reality, the various skillful means for converting sentient beings, thereby entering the various gateways of those skillful means for converting such beings.

Regarding "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā): having attained great enlightenment, one acquires a mind of equal great compassion toward all sentient beings, desiring to cause all those sentient beings to realize great enlightenment through awakening in the same manner as the realized wisdom of a Buddha.
Next, one continuously turns the great wheel of Dharma with equality toward all sentient beings without rest.
It should be understood that these three phrases are called "powers" because they are capable of benefiting others.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of these six phrases: the first three phrases refer to unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and other such qualities.
These are associated with the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and demonstrate his own benefit.
The remaining three types of phrases—namely, wisdom and so forth—demonstrate the benefit of others.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: because one possesses wisdom, one realizes the supreme, quiescent Dharmakāya; therefore, this is called self-benefit.
Furthermore, by relying on the power of compassion and so forth, as expressed in the two lines [of verse], he turns the Great Wheel of Dharma, manifesting benefit for others.
Having explained the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma is now elucidated.
Chapter 3: The Jewel of the Dharma *Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, Chapter Three: The Jewel of the Dharma The Treatise states:
Based upon that Jewel of the Buddha, there is the True Jewel of the Dharma; for this reason, immediately following the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma is manifested.
Relying upon that Jewel of the Dharma, these four verses are spoken:
Neither existent nor non-existent, Nor yet both existent and non-existent.
Neither identical to that, nor yet separate from it;
Inconceivable, beyond the sphere of wisdom derived from hearing;
Transcending the path of speech, The inner mind knows its own cool serenity.
That truly wondrous Dharma-sun, pure and free from dust and defilement,
with the radiance of great wisdom, shines universally upon all worlds.
It is able to destroy all veils and obscurations— namely, discursive thought, craving, hatred, and delusion.
I now pay homage to all afflictions and the like.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
The verse says:
Inconceivable and non-dual, Without division, purity manifests in opposition;
Depending on what, what dharma is attained? It is free from the characteristics of the two truths of dharmas.
This verse briefly clarifies the eight kinds of merit subsumed within the Jewel of the Dharma.
What are the eight? First, the inconceivable;
second, non-duality; third, non-conceptualization; fourth, purity; fifth, manifestation; sixth, the antidote; seventh, the fruit of detachment; and eighth, the cause of detachment.
Regarding "separation," the verse says:
The truths of cessation and the path, etc., Are subsumed within the two truths;
Each possesses three virtues, Which should be understood as explained in sequence.
What does this verse clarify?

Among the six preceding virtues, the first three—namely, the inconceivable, the non-dual, and the non-conceptual—should be understood as demonstrating that the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) encompasses the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).

The remaining three phrases—purity (*śuddhi*), manifestation (*vyakti*), and counteraction (*pratipakṣa*)—should be understood as demonstrating that the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) encompasses the causes for abandoning the afflictions.
Furthermore, the detachment inherent in the realization of the Dharma is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
By what dharmas is the practice that severs afflictions called the Truth of the Path?
One should know that these two truths combined constitute the dharma of purification, and the characteristics of these two truths are termed the dharma of detachment.
The verse says:
Beyond conceptualization and beyond words, it is known by the internal wisdom of the wise;
for this reason, it cannot be conceived.
The dharma of non-duality that is cool and refreshing, And the dharma of non-conceptualization,
Which is the purification and manifestation of the remedy— These three phrases are like the sun.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
It should be understood that the Truth of Cessation is briefly explained as having three kinds of dharmas;
for this reason, it is inconceivable. For what reason is it inconceivable?
It is because there are four reasons.
What are the four? First, non-existence; second, existence; third, both existence and non-existence; fourth, neither.
As the verse says:
It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent; it is neither identical to that [reality] nor distinct from it.
Regarding the statement that "one should know that there are three kinds of dharmas within the Truth of Cessation," what is the meaning of this clarification?
The Truth of Cessation cannot be known through ordinary cognition;
there are three kinds of dharmas. What are these three?
The first is because it is not within the sphere of discursive thought, as the verse says:
It cannot be conceived through deliberation, because it is not within the sphere of the wisdom derived from hearing.
Second, it is because it is far removed from all sounds, names, phrases, words, and appearances; as the verse says:
"Because it transcends the path of speech."
Third, because the Sage internally realizes the Dharma, the verse says:
"Because it is known by the inner mind.

Furthermore, regarding how the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the non-dual dharma and how it is without conceptual differentiation, as the Tathāgata said in the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa Sūtra*:
Śāriputra! The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is cool and serene because it is the non-dual dharma and because it is the non-conceptual dharma.
As the verse says:
Because it is cool and serene.
What are the two that are said to be non-dual?
The so-called "two" refers to karma and afflictions.
What is called "discrimination" refers to the accumulation of the causes of karmic activity and afflictions, as well as improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and so forth.

To know that their intrinsic nature is fundamentally quiescent, non-dual, and without duality, and to know that suffering is fundamentally unarisen—this is termed the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. It is not because of the extinction of phenomena that it is called the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Mañjuśrī! In which dharmas do mind, thought, and consciousness not function?"

Within those dharmas there is no discrimination; because there is no discrimination, false thoughts do not arise. Because there is right mindfulness, ignorance does not arise. Because ignorance does not arise, the twelve links of existence do not arise. Because the twelve links of existence do not arise, this is called "non-arising."
Therefore, the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"World-Honored One!
It is not because of the extinction of phenomena that it is called the Truth of the Extinction of Suffering."
World-Honored One!

That which is called the cessation of suffering is named beginningless, uncreated, unarisen, inexhaustible, and free from exhaustion; it is eternal, constant, cool, immutable, and pure by its very nature, being free from the entanglements of the storehouse of all afflictions.
World-Honored One!

The inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—neither separate from, nor detached from, nor different [from the dharmadhātu]—are ultimately accomplished; this is called the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
World-Honored One!
In this way, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, when not yet separated from its entanglement within the storehouse of afflictions (*kleśakośa*), is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Such matters as these should be understood as explained in detail in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Furthermore, by what cause is this Truth of Cessation, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, attained?
It should be understood that the non-conceptual wisdom within the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation possesses three types of analogies corresponding to the sun.
The verse says:
"Because it is the sun of that true and wondrous Dharma.
What are these three?
First is the analogy of the sun’s disk being pure, because it is free from all defilements of affliction (*kleśa*).
The verse says:
"Because it is pure and free from dust and dirt."
Second is the dharma of similarity and correspondence with the manifestation of all forms and images, because it can illuminate and know them through all modes and all-encompassing wisdom.
As the verse says:
"Because of the light of great wisdom."
Third is the analogous dharma of counteracting darkness, because it gives rise to the counteractive dharma of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As the verse says:
"Because it universally illuminates all worlds."
Furthermore, what are the factors to be remedied?
They are the conceptualizations and discursive thoughts based on grasping at the signs of unreal things, which give rise to the fetters and afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
What does this clarify?

Foolish ordinary beings, relying on the underlying tendencies and afflictions (*anuśaya-kleśa*), give rise to a mind of greed because they grasp at and dwell upon the signs of unreal things; they give rise to a mind of hatred because they rely on malice; and they give rise to a mind of delusion because they rely on the false conceptualizations of ignorance.

Furthermore, based on those false discriminations of greed, hatred, and delusion, one grasps at the signs of unreal phenomena and gives rise to a mind of distorted mindfulness; based on this mind of distorted mindfulness, the fetters arise; and based on these fetters, greed, hatred, and delusion arise.

For this reason, through body, speech, and mind, one performs actions of greed, hatred, and delusion; and by depending on these actions, there is further birth upon birth, uninterrupted and unceasing.

In this way, all such ignorant ordinary persons, relying on the fetters and afflictions, give rise to wrong mindfulness; relying on wrong mindfulness, they give rise to various afflictions; relying on afflictions, they give rise to all karma; and relying on karma, birth arises.
Thus, regarding all these defilements of afflictions, defilements of karma, and defilements of birth, foolish worldlings do not know or see the single true nature-realm as it truly is.
Just as that suchness is, one observes suchness without grasping at signs; because of not grasping at signs, one is able to see true nature.
This true nature is realized and known with equality by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, one does not perceive such characteristics of false and illusory phenomena, but perceives and knows them as they truly are—the true thusness and the dharma-realm that exist in reality.
Because one perceives the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), these two aspects of phenomena neither increase nor decrease; therefore, this is called the wisdom of equal realization.
These are called the dharmas that constitute the obstacles to be remedied by the knowledge of all modes; they should be understood in this way.
Because the remedial dharma of the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) has arisen, those remedied dharmas will never again arise or manifest.
The verse states:
"It is able to destroy all obscurations, such as discursive thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), greed, hatred, delusion, and all other afflictions.

Furthermore, this attainment of the *tathāgatagarbha*—the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata—is caused by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). This is explained at length in sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, which state:
Subhūti! True suchness is the Tathāgata; true suchness is equal and without differentiation.
It should be understood in this way.
Having already explained the Jewel of the Dharma, the Jewel of the Saṅgha will now be explained.
Chapter Four: The Jewel of the Saṅgha. The Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra, Chapter Four: The Jewel of the Saṅgha. The treatise states:
Based upon the Jewel of the Mahāyāna Dharma, there exists the Jewel of the Saṅgha of irreversible Bodhisattvas.
For this reason, following the Jewel of the Dharma, the Jewel of the Saṃgha is manifested.
Relying upon that Jewel of the Saṃgha, these four verses are spoken:
The Perfectly Awakened One, the one with perfect knowledge, Beholds all sentient beings.
Pure and without self, it is the tranquil reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
By being able to know that the mind is pure by nature and seeing that afflictions have no reality,
one is thus liberated from all afflictions.
Those with unobstructed, pure wisdom see sentient beings as they truly are:
their intrinsically pure nature, which is the realm of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
With the eye of unimpeded, pure wisdom, they perceive the nature of all sentient beings.
Pervading immeasurable realms, I now pay homage to you.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
The verse says:
Knowing the internal body as it truly is, With wisdom and vision purified,
Therefore it is called the Unsurpassed Saṅgha, As taught by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
The verse says:
Seeing sentient beings as they truly are, They are the quiescent, true Dharmakāya;
Because one sees that the nature is fundamentally pure, Afflictions are originally non-existent.
What does this verse clarify?
It means that one should know, through seeing reality as it is, that both the self and phenomena have been empty since the very beginning.
The verse says:
One who is perfectly awakened and possesses perfect knowledge perceives that all sentient beings are pure and devoid of self, because they are the quiescent reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Furthermore, he knows as it truly is that from beginningless time the primordial limit has been quiescent, without self and without phenomena; it is not something that comes into existence for the first time at the moment of realizing the cessation of afflictions.
What does this clarify?
This vision is the naturally pure *dharmakāya*.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of phenomena.
What are these two?
First, seeing that the nature of reality is inherently pure by its very essence; second, seeing that all afflictions are inherently quiescent from the beginning.
As the verse says:
This is because one is able to know that the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) perceives afflictions as having no reality and is free from all afflictions.

Furthermore, while the intrinsically pure mind is originally pure, it is also originally and constantly defiled by afflictions; these two types of phenomena—the virtuous mind and the non-virtuous mind—coexist within that untainted realm of *tathatā*, and there is no third mind beyond them.
This meaning is difficult to realize.
Therefore, the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:
"World-Honored One!"
A wholesome mind in a single kṣaṇa is not defiled by afflictions;
an unwholesome mind in a single kṣaṇa is likewise not defiled by afflictions.
Afflictions do not touch the mind, and the mind does not touch afflictions.
"How is it that one can have a defiled mind without contacting dharmas?
World-Honored One!
Nevertheless, there are afflictions, and there is a mind defiled by afflictions."
That the intrinsically pure mind can be defiled is difficult to comprehend.
Such matters are explained in detail in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*; one should understand both the intrinsically pure mind and its defilement by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice: practice according to reality and universal practice, both of which have meanings that are difficult to realize and know.
Practice according to reality refers to seeing that the self-nature of sentient beings is pure, for it is the realm of Buddha-nature.
The verse says:
"One with unobstructed pure wisdom perceives sentient beings as they truly are; because the nature of self-purity is the realm of the Buddha-dharmakāya.
"Universal practice" means practicing throughout all realms of the ten stages, and seeing that all sentient beings possess omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, regarding "pervading all objects": because it pervades all objects, one should know that by means of supramundane wisdom, one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha within all sentient beings, even down to animals.

He perceives that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature), because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the first stage have universally realized the entire *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*.
The verse says:
With the eye of unimpeded, pure wisdom, one perceives the nature of all sentient beings because it pervades immeasurable realms.
Thus, within one's own body, through self-awakening, one realizes that the untainted *dharmadhātu* is without obstruction or hindrance, based upon two factors:
First is practice according to reality, and second is universal practice.
What does this clarify?

It means that one should know this refers to the supramundane wisdom of the true dharma of suchness, which is internally realized according to reality and is not shared with those of the two vehicles or ordinary worldlings.
What does this clarify?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of supramundane, pure realized knowledge belonging to Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which are superior to the realized knowledge of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What are these two? First is non-obstruction, and second is non-hindrance.
As for non-obstruction, it refers to practicing according to reality and perceiving the realm of the self-nature purity of all sentient beings; therefore, it is called non-obstruction.
"Unobstructed" means practicing universally; because one knows boundless objects of experience as they truly are, it is called "unobstructed.
What does this clarify?
The verse says:
Knowing and seeing the path as it truly is, Seeing the pure wisdom of the Buddha,
The noble one does not regress, And is able to act as a refuge for sentient beings.
What meaning does this verse clarify?

Furthermore, it should be understood that by relying on the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s pure knowledge of realization in the first stage, and the vehicle of the non-retrogressive stage of the path of vision, one is able to act as the cause for the pure and supreme attainment of that unsurpassed enlightenment.
The verse says:
"Knowing and seeing the path as it truly is, because one sees the pure Buddha-wisdom.

This realization-wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*) surpasses the merits of the perfections (*pāramitā*)—such as generosity and ethical discipline—of other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. For this reason, by relying on the realization-wisdom that perceives *tathatā* (suchness) as it truly is, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings, including the eight classes of gods and dragons, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
The verse says:
Because non-regressing noble ones can act as a refuge for sentient beings.
Question:
For what reason is the refuge in the Sangha Jewel of the Śrāvakas not explained?
The answer is:
because the merit of the Bodhisattva Sangha Jewel is immeasurable, it is therefore worthy of offerings.
Because they are worthy of offerings, they should be honored with prostrations, praise, and worship.
Śrāvakas do not possess such qualities; for this reason, taking refuge in the Saṅgha Jewel of the Śrāvakas is not explicitly taught.
What does this clarify?
The verse says:
The objects, the various virtues, Realized wisdom, and nirvāṇa.
The various stages are pure and stainless, Fulfilling great compassion.
Born into the family of the Tathāgatas, Endowed with sovereign supernormal powers,
The fruit is supreme and most unsurpassed— This is the meaning of the supreme refuge.
What does this verse clarify?
Briefly stated, it clarifies that the ten kinds of supreme meanings of the bodhisattvas surpass those of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What are these ten?

First, superiority of contemplation; second, superiority of merit; third, superiority of realized wisdom; fourth, superiority of nirvāṇa; fifth, superiority of the stages; sixth, superiority of purity; seventh, superiority of the impartial mind; eighth, superiority of birth; ninth, superiority of spiritual power; and tenth, superiority of the fruit.
Regarding "superiority in contemplation": this refers to contemplating the realm of *tathatā* (suchness); this is called superiority in contemplation, as the verse states:

"because of the realm. Regarding "superiority in merit": the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of practice is insatiable, unlike the limited desires and so forth of the two vehicles; this is called superiority in merit.
The verse says:
"Because of merit.
Regarding the excellence of realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna-viśeṣa*): it refers to realizing the two kinds of selflessness; this is called the excellence of realized wisdom.
The verse says:
"Because of realized wisdom.
As for the excellence of nirvāṇa, it is because it teaches and transforms sentient beings; this is called the excellence of nirvāṇa.
The verse says:
"Because of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the excellence of the stages (*bhūmi-viśeṣa*): that which is called the ten stages and so forth is termed the excellence of the stages.
The verse says:
"Because of the various stages.
Regarding "superiority in purity": when a bodhisattva is far removed from the cognitive obscurations, this is called superiority in purity.
The verse says:
"Because it is pure and stainless.
Regarding the superiority of the impartial mind: the Bodhisattva’s great compassion pervades everywhere; this is called the superiority of the impartial mind.
The verse says:
"Because of fulfilling great compassion.
Regarding "superior birth," it refers to the fact that all bodhisattvas give birth to the non-arising [of phenomena]; this is called superior birth.
The verse says:
"Because of being born into the family of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "superiority in spiritual power" (*ṛddhiviśeṣa*): this refers to the superiority of powers such as mastery over meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); this is called superiority in spiritual power.
The verse says:
"Because of being fully endowed with mastery over samādhis and supernormal powers.
Regarding the excellence of the fruit: it is because of ultimate, unsurpassed bodhi; this is called the excellence of the fruit.
The verse says:
"Because its fruit is supreme and most unsurpassed.
What does this clarify?

There are wise people who know that the merits of all bodhisattvas are immeasurable; they cultivate the infinite and boundless, vast merits of enlightenment, possessing great wisdom and perfect compassion. To illuminate and understand the dense forest of the dispositions and conducts of those immeasurable sentient beings, they are like the new moon—except for the full moon of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that those from the śrāvakas up to those who have realized the path of arhatship are persons of little wisdom who lack great compassion; they illuminate themselves alone, like the stars.
Having understood this, one who wishes to attain the Tathāgata’s body of great full moon and cultivate the path to enlightenment must abandon the crescent moon.
It is impossible for a Bodhisattva to give rise to the thought of prostrating to or making offerings to other stars—namely, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What is the meaning of this?
It clarifies that the initial arousal of the bodhicitta is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.

Even those bodhisattvas who have already subdued themselves and practice untainted, pure precepts for their own benefit—rather than for the benefit of other sentient beings—surpass even the śrāvakas who have attained the fruit of arhatship; how much more so, then, is it impossible for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has attained the ten masteries and immeasurable, boundless merits to be equal to those of little merit, such as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? There is no such possibility.
For this reason, a verse in the sutra says:
"If one practices the prohibitive precepts for the sake of oneself alone,
being far removed from the mind of great compassion and abandoning sentient beings who have broken the precepts,"
If one guards the wealth of the precepts for the sake of oneself alone,
the Buddha says that such a keeper of the precepts is not pure.
But if one practices the precepts for the sake of others, [that is true purity].
Able to benefit sentient beings, like earth, water, fire, and wind,
for the sake of other beings, one gives rise to the foremost compassionate mind;
this is called pure upholding of the precepts, while anything else is not truly pure.
Question: Based on what meaning and for the sake of what kind of people did the Buddhas and Tathāgatas proclaim these Three Jewels? Answer:
The verse says:
Based on the Teacher, that which is realized, and the disciples of the three vehicles;
through faith in the Three Jewels, the offerings, and so forth—for these reasons, the Three Jewels are spoken of.
What does this verse clarify?
Briefly stated, the Three Jewels are taught based on three meanings for the sake of six types of persons.
What are these three?
First is the trainer, second is the method of training, and third is the disciple of the trainer.
As the verse says:
"Because of the trainer, that which is realized, and the disciple."
Regarding the six kinds of persons, what are the six?

First, those of the Mahāyāna; second, those of the Madhyamāyāna; third, those of the Hīnayāna; fourth, those who have faith in the Buddha; fifth, those who have faith in the Dharma; and sixth, those who have faith in the Saṅgha.
The verse says:
"For the sake of those who have faith in the Three Vehicles and for the sake of the three types of offerings, etc.

First, the primary meaning is explained: regarding the first and fourth persons, they take refuge in the Buddha, the most supreme and foremost among two-legged beings, because he manifests the significance of being a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa) and a Teacher who tames others. As the verse says:
Because he is the one who can discipline others,
and for the sake of those bodhisattvas who seek to attain the enlightenment of a Buddha, the verse says:
"For the sake of the Mahāyāna."
For the sake of those who, through faith, make offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, who are fields of merit, the verse says:
"Because of faith in the Buddha and making offerings.
For this reason, the Jewel of the Buddha is established; as the verse says:
Therefore, having explained the Jewel of the Buddha by means of the first meaning and the first and fourth persons, we now explain the second meaning and the second and fifth persons.
These persons take refuge in the supreme and foremost Dharma that is free from afflictions, because it manifests the qualities of the Dharma realized by the Teacher, the Tamer. Thus, the verse says:
Because they rely on what has been realized—

being those who, for the sake of the Pratyekabuddhas, know the profound principle of causes and conditions through their own spontaneous wisdom rather than through the knowledge of another— the verse says:
"For the sake of the Middle Vehicle."
Because he is a person who is a field of merit for the supreme and wondrous Dharma, worthy of being honored with faith, the verse says:
"Because of making offerings of faith to the Dharma.
For this reason, the Jewel of the Dharma is established; as the verse says:
Therefore, because of the teaching of the Jewel of the Dharma, the second meaning has already been explained for the second and fifth persons.

Next, the third meaning is explained for the third and sixth persons, who take refuge in the Sangha of Bodhisattvas—the most excellent and foremost among all assemblies—because they manifest the sense that the disciples of the Teacher, the Tathāgatas, practice in accordance with reality within the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, without contradiction. As the verse says:
Because of the disciples—
specifically those who are śrāvakas who hear from others— the verse says:
"For the sake of the Hīnayāna."
For the sake of those who, out of faith, make offerings to the foremost field of merit among the noble assembly, the verse says:
"Because of making offerings to the Sangha with faith.
For this reason, the Jewel of the Sangha is established; as the verse says:
Therefore, it is said that because of the Jewel of the Saṃgha,
the Tathāgatas have briefly explained these Three Jewels based on three meanings for the sake of six types of persons.
The verse says:

"Based on that which the Tamer has realized, the disciples are established in the three vehicles; because they have faith in the Three [Jewels], the offerings, and so forth, the Three Jewels are thus proclaimed.

Furthermore, in order to lead those beings who are capable of being transformed to enter [the path] in successive stages, for this reason, based upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the three refuges are manifested, clearly explained, and established.
What does this clarify?
The verse says:
That which is to be abandoned and that which is false, that which is non-existent and that which is fearful.
"The two kinds of Dharma and the Saṃgha are not the ultimate refuge.
What does this verse clarify?
There are two kinds of Dharma.
What are these two? First, the Dharma that is taught; second, the Dharma that is realized.
As for the Dharma that is taught, it refers to that which is comprised within the collections of names, phrases, and syllables, such as the sūtras and so forth, spoken by the Tathāgata.
The Dharma taught by him ceases at the time of realizing the Path, like abandoning a boat or a raft.
As the verse says:
"Because it is to be abandoned."
The dharmas that are realized are further of two kinds, namely, distinguished by way of cause and effect, because one realizes a certain dharma by relying upon another dharma.
What does this clarify?
That which is called "possessing the path" is subsumed by the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If it were subsumed by the characteristics of the conditioned, that phenomenon would be false.
As the verse says:

Furthermore, because they are false and illusory, if something is false and illusory, that phenomenon is not real; if it is not real, it is not the ultimate truth; if it is not the ultimate truth, it is impermanent; and if it is impermanent, it cannot be a refuge.

Furthermore, the cessation attained by relying on that path of the śrāvakas is likewise insubstantial, like the extinguishing of a lamp; it merely severs a limited portion of afflictions and suffering.
If it were thus, it would be a non-entity; if it were a non-entity, how could it serve as a refuge for others?
As the verse says:
"Because it is a non-entity."

The Sangha consists of those belonging to the three vehicles. Among these three vehicles, those who rely on the Śrāvaka Sangha always harbor fear; they constantly seek refuge in the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, seeking liberation from the world.
This is what a practitioner of the training ought to do, because it is not yet consummated and because one is still progressing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for what was called "fear," what is meant by fear?

Although an Arhat has exhausted all outflows (āsrava), he does not sever all habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of affliction; consequently, a mind of extreme dread toward all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is constantly present before him.
Therefore, the *Ārya-Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (here cited as the *Ārya-Lalitavistara-sūtra*) states:
"Arhats have fear. Why is this so?

The Arhat dwells with a sense of dread toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), as if a man were approaching with a drawn sword intent on harming him; therefore, the Arhat possesses no ultimate bliss.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Those who do not seek refuge rely upon that which is not a refuge; just as sentient beings, being without refuge, experience various terrors, and because of those terrors, they seek a place of refuge.
Thus, an arhat may possess fear; because of that terror, he takes refuge in the Tathāgata.
Therefore, if such a person possesses fear in this way, that individual ultimately seeks a state of fearlessness in order to distance himself from that state of fear.

For this reason, based on the state that is free from those fears, it is said that for a practitioner there is something yet to be accomplished: the desire to attain the state of fearlessness, which is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, the two jewels of the Śrāvaka Dharma and Saṅgha are partial refuges, not ultimate refuges.
The verse says:
"The two kinds of Dharma and the Saṃgha are not the ultimate refuge.
What does this clarify?
The verse says:
Sentient beings take refuge in one place: the Buddha, the Dharma-body, and the further shore.
Relying on the Buddha’s body is the Dharma; relying on the Dharma is the ultimate Sangha.
What does this verse clarify?

As previously stated, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are neither born nor extinguished; they are quiescent and non-dual because they possess the stainless *dharmakāya*, for they abide in the ultimate purity of the singular *dharmakāya*.

Furthermore, for those of the three vehicles who have no savior and no refuge, there is only the other shore—the beginningless primordial limit that is ultimately inexhaustible—which can be taken as a refuge and is eternally worthy of being taken as a refuge; that is to say, it is solely the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Because it is thus eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging, it is worthy of being taken as a refuge.
This should be understood as explained in detail in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*. Question:
For what reason are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha called "jewels"?
The answer is given in verse:
True jewels are rare in the world; through their brilliance, purity, and power, they are able to adorn the world, being supreme, immutable, and so forth.
What meaning does this verse clarify?

Regarding what is called "jewels," there are six kinds of similarities; because they correspond to those six kinds of similar qualities, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are spoken of as jewels.
What are these six?
First is the dharma of similarity that is difficult to obtain in the world, because sentient beings who lack roots of goodness cannot attain it even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
As the verse says:
"True jewels are rare in the world."
Second is the dharma of similarity through being stainless, because it is free from all out-flowing (āsrava) dharmas.
The verse says:
"Because it is luminous and pure."

Third is the principle of similarity through majestic power (*prabhāva*), because he possesses the inconceivable mastery of majestic power through the perfection of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
The verse says:
"Because of his power."
The fourth is the analogous dharma of adorning the world, because it is able to adorn that which transcends the world.
As the verse says: "Because it is able to adorn the world."
Fifth is the method of analogy based on superior excellence, because it pertains to supramundane dharmas.
The verse says:
"Because it is supreme."

Sixth is the dharma of being unalterable, similar, and corresponding, because having attained the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), one cannot be moved by the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*).
The verse says:
"Because it is immutable."
Question:
Based upon what dharma do these Three Jewels exist, and by depending on this dharma, how is there the arising of the pure worldly and supramundane Three Jewels?
Answer: To explain that meaning, two lines of verse are spoken:
True Suchness with defilements, And True Suchness free from all defilements.
The Buddha’s immeasurable merits, as well as the deeds performed by the Buddha—
such wondrous realms are known only to all Buddhas;
relying upon this wondrous Dharma-body, the Three Jewels are brought forth.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
The verse says:
"Such is the nature of the Three Jewels; it is the domain of the Buddhas alone."
"By means of the four dharmas in sequence, because they are inconceivable.
What does this verse clarify?
"True Suchness with impurities" refers to the Buddha-nature of True Suchness when it has not yet been freed from being entangled by the various afflictions; that is, the Tathāgatagarbha.

Furthermore, "being far removed from all defilements" means that when that very *tathāgatagarbha* transforms and reaches the stage of Buddhahood, it realizes the *dharmakāya*, which is called the "Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.

"The immeasurable merits of the Buddha" refers to all the supramundane qualities—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)—possessed within the characteristics of that transformed *tathāgatadharmakāya*, which are immeasurable and boundless.

Regarding "and the deeds performed by the Buddha": that is to say, those ten powers and all other qualities of a Buddha naturally and perpetually perform the unsurpassed deeds of a Buddha; they are always unceasing, always unremitting, and always bestow predictions of enlightenment upon all bodhisattvas.
In that place, there are four kinds of inconceivable dharmas in succession; therefore, it is called the realm of the Tathāgata.
What are these four?
The verse says:
The locus where defilement and purity correspond is undefiled yet pure;
it is a phenomenon that is never separated from them, naturally free of conceptual discrimination.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
Regarding "True Suchness with defilements," it means that within the same moment there is both purity and affliction; this state is inconceivable.
It is inconceivable because those who believe in the profound law of dependent origination—the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—do not have it as their sphere of experience.
Therefore, in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Śrīmālā:
"O Goddess!
That the intrinsically pure mind is subject to defilement is difficult to comprehend."

There are two things difficult to comprehend: namely, that the intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend, and that this very mind is defiled by afflictions is likewise difficult to comprehend.

"O Devī! These two dharmas can be heard and received only by you and by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have accomplished the Great Dharma; as for all other Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the like, they rely solely on the Buddha’s word to believe in these two dharmas."
The verse says:
"Because it is the locus where defilement and purity correspond.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having distanced oneself from all stains," *tathatā* (suchness) is not originally defiled and subsequently becomes pure; this locus is inconceivable. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The nature of the mind is intrinsically pure.
This intrinsically pure mind is primordially pure; as is the essential body of that mind, so does the Tathāgata know it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Because the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the wisdom associated with a single moment of mind,
the verse says:
"It is pure without being defiled."

The "immeasurable qualities of the Buddha" refers to the fact that from the past limit to the future limit, even while within the stage of ordinary beings who are consistently defiled, he never abandons the *tathatā*-dharmakāya; all the qualities of the Buddhas are without difference or distinction, and this state is inconceivable.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere."

Why is this? Because within the realm of all sentient beings, there is not a single being whose body does not fully possess the merits and wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because sentient beings are inverted that they do not know that the Tathāgata’s wisdom—being free from inversion—arises as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), teacherless wisdom (*anācāryaka-jñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅga-jñāna*).
O Son of the Buddha!
It is as if there were a single, immense scripture scroll equal in size to a trichiliocosm, wherein everything existing within that great trichiliocosm is recorded without exception;
if it were equal in size to a dichiliocosm, it would record all matters within that dichiliocosm.
If it is equal in size to a small thousand-world system, they record all matters within that small thousand-world system;
if it is equal to the four continents, they record all matters of all four continents;
if it is equal to Sumeru, the King of Mountains, they record all matters concerning Sumeru, the King of Mountains; and so forth.
Regarding "the palaces of the Earth Devas" and so forth, it records all matters within the palaces of the Earth Devas;
regarding "the palaces of the Desire Realm Devas" and so forth, it records all matters within the palaces of the Desire Realm Devas;
regarding "the palaces of the Form Realm Devas" and so forth, it records all matters within the palaces of the Form Realm Devas.
If it were equal in size to the celestial palaces of the formless realms, it would record all matters within the palaces of every realm in the formless world.
Those extremely large sutra scrolls of the trichiliocosm would reside within a single, most minute and subtle atom; and all atoms are likewise so.

At that time, there appeared in the world a person of wisdom and sagacity who was fully endowed with the pure divine eye. Seeing this sutra scroll within a minute particle of dust, he thought to himself:
"How is it that such a vast sutra scroll remains within a minute particle of dust without benefiting all sentient beings?"
"I should now diligently apply skillful means to break apart those atoms and bring forth this sutra scroll to benefit sentient beings.
Having formed this thought,
that person immediately applied skillful means to destroy the atoms and bring forth this sutra scroll to benefit sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!

The wisdom of the Tathāgata—the signless wisdom and unimpeded wisdom—is fully present within the bodies of sentient beings; yet, because foolish sentient beings are shrouded by inverted perceptions, they do not know it, do not see it, and do not give rise to faith.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure divine eye, surveyed the bodies of all sentient beings.
Having completed this observation, he spoke these words:
"How marvelous, how marvelous!
"How is it that the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom resides within their bodies yet they do not know or see it?

I shall employ skillful means to instruct those sentient beings so that they may awaken to the Noble Path, causing them all to forever leave behind the defilements and fetters of all deluded thoughts and inversions, and enabling them to fully perceive the Tathāgata’s wisdom within their own bodies, no different from that of a Buddha."

The Tathāgata immediately instructed those sentient beings to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, so that they might abandon all false and inverted views; having abandoned such inversions, they perceive the wisdom of the Tathāgata and, being equal to the Tathāgata, benefit sentient beings.
The verse says:
"Because it is a dharma that is never separated [from them].

Furthermore, regarding the Buddha's activities: at one and the same time, in all places, and at all times, they occur spontaneously and without discrimination. In accordance with the minds of sentient beings and in accordance with the capacities and natures of those to be converted, he performs the Buddha-activities in a way that is unfailing and unerring. This point is inconceivable.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"O son of good family!
In order to cause all sentient beings to enter into the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata expresses the immeasurable activities of a Tathāgata through finite descriptions."
Good son! All the actual deeds performed by the Tathāgata are, for all sentient beings in the world, immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, unknowable, and cannot be described by names.

Why is this? Because it is difficult to attain for sentient beings as they have existed from before; because it does not cease throughout all Buddha-lands; because all Buddhas are entirely equal; because it transcends all mental activities of the mundane world; because it is non-conceptual and entirely equal like space; and because its essence is the dharma-nature, which is without distinction or differentiation.
Having thus explained at length, he further spoke the analogy of the impure great Vaiḍūrya mani-jewel, saying:
"Good son!

Relying on this analogy, you should know that because the karma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, because it is impartial and all-pervading, because it cannot be censured in any place, because it is equal throughout the three periods of time, and because it ensures the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed, although the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, abide within such inconceivable karma, they do not abandon the space-like Dharma-body."
Although he does not abandon the space-like Dharma-body, he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings according to the names and phrases they should hear.
Although he thus preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, he remains constantly detached from all mental observations and conceptualizations of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they know, as it truly is, the mental activities of all sentient beings.
As the verse says:
Because it is naturally non-conceptual.
Regarding how the Three Jewels arise from this sublime Dharma-body, the verse says:
The Dharma of enlightenment that is realized Is known by means of the factors of enlightenment.
The teaching of the factors of enlightenment brings sentient beings to the awakening of bodhi.
The first phrase constitutes the direct cause; the remaining three are the purifying conditions.
The former two pertain to one's own benefit, while the latter two pertain to the benefit of others.
What does this verse clarify?
These four phrases comprehensively encompass the entire range of all that can be known.
What does this clarify?
Regarding the first phrase, it refers to the dharma to be realized, which should be known; for that dharma of realization is called bodhi.
As the verse says:
"Because it is the dharma of bodhi to be awakened to."

Regarding the second phrase, "knowing the basis of enlightenment through the factors of enlightenment," this is because the merits of the Buddhas' enlightenment can serve as the causes for the enlightenment of a Buddha.
The verse says:
"Because of knowing the basis of enlightenment through the factors of enlightenment."
The third phrase, "teaching through the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*), refers to causing others to awaken by means of the factors of enlightenment.
The fourth phrase, "sentient beings awakening to enlightenment," refers to the sentient beings who are to be converted awakening to enlightenment.

One should understand that by not grasping at the characteristics of these four kinds of phrases in their proper sequence and by practicing accordingly, the pure awakening gives rise to the Three Jewels.
As the verse says:
"The dharma of awakening that is realized is known through the factors of awakening; the teaching of the factors of awakening is for the sake of awakening sentient beings."
By means of one phrase as the cause and three phrases as the conditions, the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By virtue of having attained bodhi, he possesses the ten powers and other dharmas of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as well as the thirty-two kinds of activities of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

Based on the activity of the Tathāgata, sentient beings hear his voice; by relying on that Dharma, they obtain the causes and conditions for purification and give rise to the Three Jewels—this should be understood.
Therefore, the verse says:
"The first phrase is the direct cause, while the remaining three are the purifying conditions."
The Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra, Scroll Two.
The Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati of Central India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
5. All Sentient Beings Possess the Tathāgata-garbha: Chapter Five.
The Commentary states:
From this point forward, the remaining verses of the treatise should be understood as explaining, in successive order, the extensive distinctions based upon those four lines.
What is the meaning of this?
As the preceding verse states:
"True Suchness with its admixture of defilements, and [True Suchness] far removed from all defilements."
The Buddha’s immeasurable merits and the deeds performed by the Buddha—
such wondrous realms as these are known only to the Buddhas.
Relying upon this wondrous Dharma-body, the Three Jewels are brought forth.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
As previously stated, all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Based on what meaning is it so said?
The verse says:
The Buddha’s Dharma-body is all-pervading; Suchness is without differentiation;
All truly possess Buddha-nature; Therefore, it is said that [Buddhahood] is eternally present.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
There are three meanings; therefore, the Tathāgata taught that at all times all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*.
What are these three?
First, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata pervades the bodies of all sentient beings; as the verse says:
"Because the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is all-pervasive.
Second, the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata is without differentiation; as the verse says:
Because True Suchness (tathatā) is without differentiation.
Third, all sentient beings truly and universally possess the Buddha-nature of True Suchness; as the verse says:
"All truly possess the Buddha-nature."
Regarding the meaning of these three phrases, it should be understood that they will be explained by me later in this treatise based on the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*.
As the verse states:
"The realm of all sentient beings Is never separate from the wisdom of the Buddhas."
Because that purity is stainless and its essential nature is non-dual,
by relying upon the equal Dharma-nature body of all Buddhas,
one knows that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha.
The essence, cause, fruit, and activity; The correspondence and the practice;
The distinctions of time, pervasiveness, And the unchanging non-differentiation— These are the sequence of the sublime meaning, The foremost, true *dharmatā*.
"I have thus briefly explained; you should now understand it well.
What meaning does this verse reveal?

It should be understood that this verse briefly explains ten kinds of meanings; based on these ten kinds, one should know the distinctions of the Buddha-nature within the realm of the ultimate true wisdom.
What are the ten? First, essence;
second, cause; third, fruit; fourth, activity; fifth, association; sixth, practice; seventh, distinction of time; eighth, pervasiveness of all places; ninth, immutability; tenth, non-differentiation.
First, a verse is spoken based on the cause of the essence:
Its intrinsic nature is eternally unstained, Like a jewel, space, and pure water;
Faith in the Dharma, Prajñā, Samādhi, Great Compassion, and so forth.
What meaning does this first half-verse reveal?
The verse says:
Sovereign power is unchanging; its essential substance is contemplative and supple.
The qualities of the jewel, space, and water are analogous and correspond to one another.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
The three meanings previously explained follow, in their respective order, the particular and universal characteristics [of the three natures].
It should be understood that the three kinds of pure qualities of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body correspond respectively to the simile of the wish-fulfilling jewel, space, and pure water.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that because the one who contemplates relies upon the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, all that is contemplated and all that is cultivated are fully accomplished.
What meaning does the latter half of the verse demonstrate?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of obstacles: slandering the Dharma, attachment to the self, fear of worldly suffering, and abandoning all sentient beings.
What does this verse clarify?
The verse says:
"The heretics and outsiders, the śrāvakas and the self-awakened ones,"
"The four dharmas, beginning with faith, should be known as the causes of purification.
What is the meaning clarified by this verse?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of sentient beings within the entire realm of sentient beings.
What are the three?
First, seeking existence; second, distancing oneself from seeking existence; third, not seeking either of those two.
Regarding seeking existence, there are two kinds.
What are these two?
First, they slander the path of liberation as lacking the nature of nirvāṇa, constantly seeking to remain in the world and not seeking to realize nirvāṇa.
Second, within the Buddha-dharma, they occupy the same station as icchantikas because they slander the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Śāriputra!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who give rise to one view or two views, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are not their World-Honored Ones; such persons as these are not my disciples."

Śāriputra! Because these people give rise to the causes and conditions of dualistic views, they pass from darkness into darkness and from obscurity into obscurity; it is for this reason that I call them icchantikas.
The verse says:
"Because of slandering the Dharma and because of the icchantikas.
There are likewise two kinds of those who distance themselves from seekers of existence.
What are these two?
First, the absence of skillful means for seeking the Path; second, the presence of skillful means for seeking the Path.
Regarding the absence of skillful means for seeking the Path, there are likewise two kinds.
What are these two?

First, there are the various heterodox teachers with their manifold false speculations—namely, the Sāṃkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, the Nirgrantha Jñātiputras, and others—who lack the skillful means for seeking the Way.
Second, those who within the Buddha-dharma practice in the same manner as non-Buddhists; though they have faith in the Buddha-dharma, they grasp it erroneously.
What are these people?

They are those such as the Vātsīputrīyas who perceive a self within the body; they do not believe in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) nor do they believe in the emptiness of dharmas as suchness (tathatā). The Buddha said that such people are no different from non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, there are those who reckon emptiness as being existent because of their pride in the mark of a self. Why is this?
Although the Tathāgata has taught the gate of liberation that is emptiness so that they might attain awakening and understanding, those people reckon that it is merely empty and lacks reality.
For the sake of such people, the Buddha told Kāśyapa in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*:
"It would be better to perceive a self as large as Mount Sumeru than to perceive an arrogant being who regards emptiness as existent."
Kāśyapa! All false views are abandoned through the realization of emptiness.
If one perceives emptiness as an existent thing, that person cannot be transformed to leave the world behind.
The verse says:
"And because of attachment to a self;
and because of [the views of] non-Buddhists."
There are also two kinds of those who seek the Way through skillful means. What are these two?
The first is the śrāvaka; as the verse says:
Because of fear of the suffering of the world, they are called Śrāvakas.
Second are the Pratyekabuddhas; as the verse says:
because of abandoning all sentient beings and because of self-awakening.
Those who seek neither of those two are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sentient beings of the foremost sharp faculties. Why is this?

It is because these bodhisattvas do not seek existence like the icchantikas; nor are they the same as the various non-Buddhists who seek the Way without skillful means; nor are they the same as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who seek the Way with skillful means.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas perceive the path of the world and the path of nirvāṇa as equal.

Because they do not dwell in a mind fixed upon nirvāṇa, and because worldly dharmas cannot defile them, they practice worldly deeds while remaining firm in their compassion and the mind of nirvāṇa, being well-established within the fundamentally pure dharma.

Furthermore, those sentient beings who seek existence—namely the icchantikas—and those within the Buddha-dharma who occupy the same rank as icchantikas, are called sentient beings of the fixed category of the heterodox (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).

Moreover, among those who have distanced themselves from seeking existence, those who fall into seeking the Way without skillful means are called sentient beings of the indeterminate category (aniyata-rāśi).

Furthermore, among those sentient beings who have distanced themselves from the pursuit of existence, those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who seek the path through the expedient means of renouncing the world, as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not seek those two [paths] but seek the wisdom of the equal path—these are called sentient beings of the group of right determination (*samyaktvaniyatarāśi*).
Furthermore, setting aside those sentient beings who seek the Mahāyāna path of non-obstruction, there are four other types of sentient beings.
What are these four?
First, the icchantikas; second, the followers of external paths; third, the śrāvakas; and fourth, the pratyekabuddhas.
Because those four types of sentient beings have four kinds of obstructions, they are unable to realize, unable to encounter, and unable to see the nature of the Tathāgata.
What are these four?
The first is the obstacle of the icchantika who slanders the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The remedy for this obstacle is the faith of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the Mahāyāna.
As the verse says:
Because of faith in the Dharma.
Second, there is the obstacle of various non-Buddhists who erroneously conceive that there is a self within the body;
the remedy for this obstacle is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The verse says:
"And because of [the lack of] prajñā.
Third is the obstacle for śrāvakas, which is the fear of the sounds of all worldly sufferings.
The remedy for this obstacle consists in the practice of various samādhis by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, such as the Gaganagañja and Śūraṅgama samādhis.
As the verse says:
"Because of samādhi."
Fourth is the obstacle of the pratyekabuddha, which consists of turning one's back on the benefit of all sentient beings and abandoning the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The remedy for this obstacle is that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice great compassion for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The verse says:
"Because of great compassion.
These are called the four kinds of obstacles, which obstruct the four kinds of sentient beings.

In order to counteract those four kinds of obstacles, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the four kinds of remedial dharmas, such as faith in the Mahāyāna; thereby they attain the unsurpassed, pure *dharmakāya* and reach the foremost shore.
Why is this? Because by practicing wholesome dharmas based on these four kinds of pure dharma-realm, one becomes a son of the Buddha who follows the Buddhas and is born into the Buddha-family.
Therefore, the verse says:
Faith in the Mahāyāna is the father, Prajñā is the mother, Dhyāna is the womb and great compassion is the milk; Thus, all Buddhas are true sons.
The verse says:
One should know that the four dharmas, beginning with faith, are the causes for purification.
Furthermore, based on the fruit and the activity, one verse is spoken:
"Purity, self, bliss, permanence, and so forth, Are the fruits of the virtues of the other shore;
Weariness with suffering and the seeking of nirvāṇa, As well as desires, vows, and various karmas.
What meaning does this first half-verse reveal?
The verse says:
To briefly explain the meaning of the four lines: the four kinds of inverted dharmas are inverted within the Dharmakāya;
one practices the remedial dharmas [to counteract them].
What is the meaning elucidated by this verse?
Those four dharmas, beginning with faith, enable the purification of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

Regarding the four types of dharmas mentioned previously, they are briefly explained in sequence as the remedies for the four inversions; it should be understood that these are the fruits of the four kinds of *pāramitās* which constitute the virtues of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
The verse says:
"Because it briefly explains the meaning of the four propositions.
What does this clarify?

That is to say, to give rise to the notion of permanence regarding impermanent phenomena such as form; to give rise to the notion of pleasure regarding suffering phenomena; to give rise to the notion of self regarding what is non-self; and to give rise to the notion of purity regarding what is impure—these should be known as the four types of perversions.
The verse states:
"Because of the four kinds of inverted phenomena.
To counteract these four kinds of inversions, one should know that there are four kinds of non-inverted phenomena.
What are the four?

They are the cultivation of the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception of impurity regarding impermanent phenomena such as form; these should be known as the four kinds of non-erroneous antidotes.
The verse says:
"Because one practices the remedial dharmas.
One should know that these four kinds of perversions, which serve as remedies [for other perversions], are themselves perversions based upon the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya.
The verse states:
"Because of inversion regarding the dharmakāya.
To counteract this inversion, it is taught that there are four kinds of fruits of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya perfections (pāramitā).
What are the four?
They are the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the purity of the perfection [of phenomena]; these should be known.
As the verse says:
Because one practices the remedial dharmas,
the *Āryaśrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"World-Honored One!..."

Ordinary beings give rise to perverted perceptions regarding the phenomena of the five aggregates: they perceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.
World-Honored One!
Those Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas who possess knowledge of emptiness have never before seen the realm of omniscience or the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
If there are sentient beings who, out of faith in the Buddha’s words, conceive of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as permanent, blissful, self, and pure—World-Honored One!
Those sentient beings do not hold perverted views; this is called right view.
Why is this? Because only the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the perfection of purity.
"Bhagavān!
If there are sentient beings who form such a view regarding the Buddha’s Dharma-body, this is called right view,
Bhagavān!"

One who possesses right view is a true child of the Buddha; born from the Buddha’s mouth, born from the True Dharma, and born through transformation by the Dharma, they have obtained the remaining wealth of the Dharma—for such reasons as these.
Furthermore, these four kinds of Tathāgata-dharmakāya qualities—the pāramitās—should be understood as being taught in sequence from cause toward fruit as purity, self, bliss, and permanence.
How is it that they proceed in sequence from cause toward fruit?
This refers to the obstacle of the icchantika who slanders the Mahāyāna; although there is in reality no purity, their minds delight in and cling to worldly purity.

The remedy for this obstacle should be understood as the Mahāsattva Bodhisattvas’ faith in the Mahāyāna, through which they practice and realize the fruit of the supreme perfection of purity (śuddhi-pāramitā).

The obstacle of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who perceive a self (*ātman*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), consists in their attachment to and grasping of a self despite the fact that no such self truly exists.

The remedy for this obstacle is as follows: it should be understood that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they realize the fruit of the foremost perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*).
What does this clarify?

All non-Buddhists (tīrthika) cling to unreal things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, asserting them to be a self (*ātman*). Yet those non-Buddhists grasp at the characteristics of a self; such characteristics of a self do not exist, being false and inverted. At all times, there is no self.
For this reason, it is said that the Tathāgata, through his knowledge of reality as it is, knows that all phenomena are selfless and has reached the supreme further shore;
yet, for the Tathāgata, there is neither "self" nor the characteristic of "selflessness."
Why is this? Because at all times one perceives and knows things as they truly are, without falsehood and without inversion.
What is the meaning of this?
To say that there is no self is precisely what is meant by saying there is a self.
That which is "no self" refers to the absence of that false, illusory *ātman* of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
That which is called "having a self" refers to the Tathāgata’s possession of that sovereign, independent self.
Therefore, the verse says:
Just as pure emptiness Attains the supreme non-self, The Buddhas attain the pure essence;
This is called attaining the Great Body.
What does this verse clarify?
"Attaining the great body" means that the Tathāgata attains the first, most pure *dharmakāya* of true suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the true self (*ātman*) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, because they have attained the essence of mastery and have attained the first, most pure body.
The verse says:
Because all Buddhas have attained the pure body.
For this reason, all Buddhas are said to have attained pure sovereignty.
The verse says:
"This is called attaining the Great Body.
For this reason, based on this meaning, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain the state of being the foremost and supreme sovereign self within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).

Furthermore, based on this very principle, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not called "existent," because it is devoid of the mark of self and the mark of phenomena. For this reason, one cannot say it exists, as such marks are non-existent in that manner.

Furthermore, based on this very meaning, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not called non-existent; because there exists only that essence of the self which is True Suchness (tathatā), one cannot say that the Dharma-body does not exist, for it exists in accordance with its characteristics.
Based on this meaning, various non-Buddhists ask:
"Does the Tathāgata have a body after death, or does he not have a body?
Because such questions arise, the Tathāgata neither records nor answers them.

Śrāvakas fear the suffering of the world; as an antidote to that fear of worldly suffering, it should be understood that because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice all mundane and supramundane samādhis, they realize the fruit of the foremost perfection of bliss.

Pratyekabuddhas abandon the welfare of all sentient beings and delight in dwelling in tranquility; as an antidote to such abandonment of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice great compassion, dwelling for limitless eons in the world to constantly benefit sentient beings, and it should be understood that they realize the fruit of the supreme, eternal *pāramitā*.

This is called the fourfold practice of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—faith, prajñā, samādhi, and great compassion. It should be understood that through this sequence, they attain the fruit of the four pāramitās of the Tathāgata’s body: purity, selfhood, bliss, and permanence.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: based on these four kinds of Tathāgata-dharmakāya, it is said to be "as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and extending to the end of the future."
What does this clarify?

It means that by practicing with faith in the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, constantly attain the pure Dharma-realm and reach the supreme other shore; therefore, it is said that they are "vast as the Dharma-realm.
By practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, achieve the space-like Dharma-body.

Because the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is ultimately without self, and because one practices immeasurable samādhis such as the Gaganagañja (Space-Treasury), by virtue of this principle, one attains mastery over all phenomena in all places; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is ultimately like space.
By practicing great compassion, one attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings at all times without limit; therefore, it is said that this extends to the end of the future.
Furthermore, these four kinds of pāramitās and so forth abide within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).

Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain great power and mastery therein, Bodhisattvas encounter four kinds of obstacles when seeking to realize the Tathāgata’s dharma-body, the supreme *pāra* (the further shore).

What are the four? First, the characteristic of conditions; second, the characteristic of causes; third, the characteristic of arising; and fourth, the characteristic of destruction. Regarding the characteristic of conditions:

this refers to the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*). This ground of abiding ignorance acts as a condition for formative forces (*saṃskāra*), just as ignorance conditions formative forces; the conditioning of the ground of abiding ignorance is likewise so.

Regarding the characteristic of cause: it refers to the unconditioned ignorance-abode (*avidyā-āvasthā*) taking formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition; that is, this very ignorance-abode takes formative forces as its cause, just as formative forces take consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their condition, and the same applies to the conditioning of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).

Regarding the characteristic of arising: it refers to the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) which arise with the ground of the dwelling of ignorance as their condition and support and with outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karman*) as their cause. This is because, just as the three realms arise with the four kinds of grasping as their condition and support and with outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karman*) as their cause, the arising of the three kinds of mind-made bodies is likewise.

Regarding the characteristic of disintegration: it refers to the inconceivable death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) associated with the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). Just as there is old age and death based on the condition of birth, so too is it with the inconceivable death of transformation associated with the three types of mind-made bodies.

Furthermore, all defilements of the afflictions are based upon the root of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). Because they do not depart from the ground of abiding ignorance, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power have not yet distanced themselves from the impurities of the ground of abiding ignorance; therefore, they have not yet attained the ultimate, unconditioned purity of the *pāramitā*.

Furthermore, based precisely on that ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), because the habitual tendencies of subtle conceptual proliferation have not yet been eternally extinguished, one has therefore not yet attained the ultimate unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, conditioned by that very ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), there is a subtle accumulation of conceptual proliferation regarding signs; because of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), the mental aggregate (*manomaya-skandha*) arises and has not yet attained permanent cessation. Therefore, one has not yet attained the ultimate unconditioned bliss of the *pāramitā*.

Because the defilements of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilements of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilements of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*) have not yet attained permanent extinction, one has therefore not realized the ultimate nectar-like *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.

Because one has not yet distanced oneself from inconceivable transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) and remains perpetually non-ultimate, one has therefore not attained the immutable essence (*avikāra-vastu*).
Therefore, one has not yet attained the ultimate, unconditioned, and eternal *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, as it is with the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), so it is with the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
As it is with the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), so it is with the practice of outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma-saṃskāra*).
Just as with birth and defilement, so it is with the three kinds of mind-made bodies and the inconceivable transformation-death.
As stated in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"O Bhagavān!"
"Just as the three realms of existence arise from the cause of tainted karma conditioned by grasping,
so too, World-Honored One,
the three kinds of mind-made bodies— those of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and powerful Bodhisattvas— arise from the cause of untainted karma conditioned by the ground of the abiding of ignorance."
"Bhagavān!

These three types of mind-made bodies produced on the stages of the Three Vehicles, as well as those produced by untainted karma, depend upon the ground of the abiding of ignorance; they have conditions and are not without conditions."
These points should be understood as explained in detail within the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

Furthermore, because the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*)—those of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and powerful bodhisattvas—lack the body of merit consisting of the perfections of purity, self, bliss, and permanence, the noble *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
