Within the realm of sentient beings, there is not a single being who exists apart from the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body outside of that Dharma-body, nor one who exists apart from the Tathāgata’s wisdom outside of that wisdom; it is just as various forms and images do not exist apart from space.
Therefore, the verse says:
Just as all forms and images do not exist apart from space,
so too the bodies of sentient beings do not exist apart from the wisdom of the Buddhas.
For these reasons, it is said that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha, just like forms within space;
because its nature is immutable and its essence is primordially pure.
"Just as true gold does not change, Therefore, True Suchness (tathatā) is used as a metaphor.
What does this verse clarify?

It clarifies that the nature of the Tathāgata, which is True Suchness, is identical and without distinction even within the bodies of sentient beings belonging to the category of the utterly depraved; it is luminous and clearly manifest because it is free from adventitious afflictions.

Later, it is stated that the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is like this: by means of the analogy of a single piece of pure gold, because *tathatā* is undifferentiated and not separate from the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*), it is said that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is because, although the intrinsically pure mind is described as "pure," it is fundamentally non-dual with respect to phenomena.
Therefore, in a sutra, the Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī!

The Tathāgata knows and perceives the fundamental wisdom of his own self as it truly is; because he relies upon this fundamental wisdom of his own self, he knows that all sentient beings possess a pure body."
Mañjuśrī! That which is called the Tathāgata’s body of intrinsic purity, and even the bodies of all sentient beings of intrinsic purity—these two dharmas are non-dual and without distinction.
Therefore, the verse says:
All sentient beings Possess the Tathāgatagarbha equally;
The pure dharma of True Suchness Is called the essence of the Tathāgata.
Based on this meaning, it is said:
"All sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha; one should know it thus.
Furthermore, a verse says:
The Buddha-nature is of two kinds:
first, like a treasure hidden in the earth; second, like the fruit of a tree.
Since beginningless time, the intrinsically pure mind has been cultivated through the practice of the unsurpassed path.
Based on the two kinds of Buddha-nature, one attains the three kinds of bodies.
By virtue of the first analogy, one knows there is the primary Dharmakāya;
by virtue of the second analogy, one knows there are the two [other] Buddha-bodies.
The true Buddha’s Dharma-body is pure, like an image of pure gold;
because its nature is unchanging, it encompasses the reality of all merits.
Having realized the rank of the Great Dharma King, it is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
"Depending upon the substance of a mirror-image, a manifested Buddha-image appears.
What does this verse clarify?

It shows that through the remaining five similes—namely, the treasury, the tree, the golden image, the wheel-turning sage king, and the precious statue—the Dharma-body of those three Buddhas is manifested.
Because all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata-nature as their own intrinsic essence, it is said that all sentient beings have the Tathāgatagarbha.
What is the meaning demonstrated by this?

Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, receive their names and meanings by virtue of possessing three kinds of bodies, these five metaphors can serve as the causes for the three kinds of Buddha-bodies; for this reason, they are called the "causes of the Tathāgata-nature."
In what sense is this?
Herein, the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*) is intended as the meaning of "cause. For this reason, a verse in the sutra says:
"The nature that has existed since beginningless time Acts as the support for all phenomena."
"Based on this nature, there are the various paths, as well as the realization of the fruit of nirvāṇa.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
Regarding "the nature of the world without beginning," it is as the Sūtra says:
The Tathāgatas, relying upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, teach that the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of all sentient beings cannot be known.
Regarding what is called "nature" (*prakṛti*), as stated in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"World-Honored One!"

When the Tathāgata speaks of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is the treasury of the *dharmadhātu*, the treasury of the supramundane *dharmakāya*, the supreme treasury of the supramundane, and the treasury of the *dharmakāya* of intrinsic purity; for the *tathāgatagarbha* is intrinsically pure by nature.
Regarding its being the support for all phenomena, as stated in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"World-Honored One!
Therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha is the support, the sustenance, the foundation, and the establishment."
World-Honored One!
It is not separate from non-separation, it is uninterrupted, unliberated, undifferentiated, unconditioned, and inconceivable—the Buddha-dharma.
World-Honored One!

Furthermore, there are conditioned phenomena that are subject to cessation, disjunction, difference, external separation, and detachment from wisdom; these also depend upon, are supported by, are sustained by, and are established in the Tathāgatagarbha.
Regarding the statement that "the various paths exist in dependence upon nature," it is as stated in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"World-Honored One,
birth and death depend upon the Tathāgatagarbha."
"World-Honored One!
Because there is the *tathāgatagarbha*, one speaks of birth and death; this is called a well-spoken teaching.
Furthermore, regarding those who realize the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, as stated in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*:"
World-Honored One!
It is because of the Tathāgatagarbha that there is birth and death; it is because of the Tathāgatagarbha that one realizes nirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
If there were no *tathāgatagarbha*, one would not be able to feel weary of suffering or joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*; this is because one would neither desire nor aspire for *nirvāṇa*.
What does this clarify?

One should know that the Tathāgatagarbha is ultimately non-different from the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; it is the essence and characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā), the definitively established nature of Buddhahood, which exists at all times within the bodies of all sentient beings without exception.
How is this known? It is known through the characteristics of the dharma.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Good son!

This dharma-nature, this dharma-essence, and this self-nature are eternally abiding. Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this self-nature is pure and has been eternally abiding from the beginning; all sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha."
What does this clarify?

Based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the essence of phenomena (*dharmatva*), the correspondence of phenomena (*dharma-saṃprayoga*), and the skillful means of phenomena (*dharma-upāya*), whether these phenomena are thus or not thus is inconceivable.

In all instances, relying on the Dharma, relying on the measure of the Dharma, and relying on faith in the Dharma, one attains purity of mind and concentration of mind; can that be distinguished as real or unreal?
Relying solely on faith in the Tathāgata,
the verse says:
Relying solely on faith in the Tathāgata, one has faith in the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
"Just as one who lacks eyesight cannot see the solar disk.
What does this verse clarify?
Briefly stated, within the entire realm of sentient beings there are four kinds of beings who do not recognize the Tathāgatagarbha, like those born blind.
What are these four?
First, ordinary persons; second, śrāvakas; third, pratyekabuddhas; and fourth, bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain awakening.
As it is said in the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"World-Honored One,
the Tathāgatagarbha is not within the sphere of experience for sentient beings who hold to the view of a self."
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is not within the sphere of those sentient beings who grasp at the four inversions.
World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgatagarbha is not within the realm of those sentient beings whose minds are distracted and who have lost the realization of emptiness.

What does this clarify? Those with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) refer to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Because these worldlings falsely grasp at the five aggregates—form and so forth—which in reality do not exist, as being "I" and "mine," they are characterized by false attachment and pride regarding "I" and "mine. They are unable to even have faith in the Dharma of the deathless, the untainted nature of the Truth of Cessation which is free from the view of a self; how much less could they realize or understand the Tathāgatagarbha, the realm of all-transcendent wisdom? Such a thing is impossible.

Furthermore, regarding those sentient beings who grasp at the four inversions—namely, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—it is because these Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others ought to practice the Tathāgatagarbha as permanent, yet they do not practice the Tathāgatagarbha as permanent; instead, through inverted grasping, they take all phenomena to be impermanent and practice the impermanence of the Tathāgatagarbha, delighting in the practice of impermanence due to their lack of knowledge and lack of awakening.

One should practice the bliss of the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet one does not practice the *tathāgatagarbha* as bliss; because of inverted grasping, one perceives all phenomena as suffering and practices the suffering of the *tathāgatagarbha*. This practice of taking suffering as bliss occurs because of a lack of knowledge and realization.

One should practice the Tathāgatagarbha as the self, yet one does not practice the Tathāgatagarbha as the self; because of grasping at all phenomena as being without self through inversion, one practices the non-self of the Tathāgatagarbha and delights in the practice of non-self, due to lack of knowledge and lack of realization.

One should practice the purification of the *tathāgatagarbha*, yet one does not practice the purification of the *tathāgatagarbha* because of grasping all phenomena as impure through inversion; thus, one practices the impurity of the *tathāgatagarbha* and delights in impure practice due to lack of knowledge and lack of awakening.
Thus, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others are all unable to practice in accordance with the Dharma-body as it truly is.
For this reason, the supreme other shore—the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity—is not within the cognitive domain of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Such inverted perceptions as taking what is impermanent to be permanent, what is suffering to be pleasure, what is non-self to be self, and what is impure to be pure, do not constitute the sphere of that Tathāgatagarbha.
This meaning is explained extensively in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* through the analogy of the pond water; this point should be understood.
That sūtra states:
"Kāśyapa! It is like this:
suppose in the springtime, there are people bathing in a great pond and playing on boats who lose a lapis lazuli gem, which sinks into the deep water."

At that time, all the people entered the water together to search for this treasure; they vied with one another to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and gravel, each claiming to have found a lapis lazuli bead. They joyfully brought them out, only to realize they were not genuine.

At that time, the precious jewel was still within the water; by the power of the jewel, the water became entirely clear and transparent, so that the great assembly could see the jewel still beneath the surface, just as one looks up at the form of the moon in the sky.
At that time, there was a wise person among the multitude who, through the power of skillful means, entered the water calmly and slowly, and immediately obtained the jewel.
You, bhikṣus!

You should not cultivate and accumulate notions of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as if they were ultimate realities, like those people who each took tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, or gravel for precious jewels. You should skillfully learn skillful means and constantly cultivate the notions of self, permanence, bliss, and purity in every place and at all times.

Furthermore, you should know that the characteristics of the four dharmas previously cultivated and accumulated are all inverted. If one wishes to attain reality and cultivate various perceptions, it is like that wise person skillfully extracting a precious jewel—namely, the perception of self, permanence, bliss, and purity.

Furthermore, regarding sentient beings who lose emptiness due to a distracted mind: this refers to bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds but are separated from the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Because they practice by means of things that are subject to loss and transformation, this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
In what sense is this?
A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment gives rise to such a thought:
"There truly exists a dharma that, through its cessation, attains nirvana at a later time."
In this way, such bodhisattvas lose the practice of the *tathāgatagarbha* as emptiness.
Furthermore, there are those who regard emptiness as a substantial entity and think, "I should attain emptiness.
They also give rise to such thoughts:
They think that there is a separate emptiness apart from phenomena such as form, and that they should practice in order to attain that emptiness.
Such people do not know that emptiness is, in fact, the *tathāgatagarbha* through which all phenomena exist.
The verse says:
The non-empty Tathāgatagarbha refers to the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas;
they possess the characteristic of being inseparable, without a single dharma being added or subtracted.
The Tathāgata’s unconditioned body, Its self-nature is primordially pure;
Defiled by adventitious, false dust, Its original self-nature is empty.
What meaning does this verse clarify?
"Not diminishing a single dharma" means not diminishing afflictions.
"Not augmenting a single dharma" means that within the nature of *tathatā*, one does not augment a single dharma,
because its pure essence is never abandoned or departed from.
The verse says:
"The characteristic of being inseparable, because not a single dharma is increased or diminished.
Therefore, the noble *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"Bhagavān!
There are two kinds of the Tathāgata-garbha’s wisdom of emptiness.
Bhagavān!"
The empty tathāgatagarbha is that which is separated from, liberated from, and distinct from the storehouse of all afflictions.
World-Honored One,

the non-empty tathāgatagarbha is so called because it contains inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable from, not liberated from, and not distinct from [the tathāgata].
Thus, to see and know as it truly is which afflictions are absent and in what locations they are absent is called the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Furthermore, to see and know as it truly is which Buddha-dharmas are fully present and in what locations they are fully present is called the knowledge of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā-jñāna*).
Thus, these two verses clarify that one should know the characteristic of emptiness as it truly is, free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, if sentient beings are separated from such wisdom of emptiness, they stand outside the realm of the Buddhas; they are said to be "inappropriate," failing to attain meditative concentration or single-mindedness. For this reason, they are called sentient beings with distracted minds who have lost emptiness.
Why is this? Because apart from the gateway of the wisdom of ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the non-conceptual realm cannot be realized or perceived.
Therefore, the noble *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
World-Honored One!
The wisdom of the Tathāgatagarbha is called the wisdom of emptiness.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha-wisdom of emptiness is that which all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others have never seen before, never attained before, never realized before, and never comprehended before.
"World-Honored One!
The extinction of all suffering is realized only by the Buddha, because he has destroyed the storehouse of all afflictions and cultivated the path that extinguishes all suffering.
Thus, this Tathāgatagarbha, being the storehouse of the Dharma-realm, cannot be seen by sentient beings who possess the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the like."
It has already been stated that because the true dharma-realm, which serves as the antidote to the view of a self-identity, has not yet manifested;
furthermore, this supramundane dharmakāya-tathāgatagarbha is not within the sphere of experience of sentient beings who are subject to inversion.
It has already been explained that because worldly phenomena such as impermanence are used as antidotes, the supramundane dharmadhātu does not manifest.
Furthermore, this naturally pure dharmadhātu, the Tathāgata-garbha, is not the domain of sentient beings whose minds are distracted and who have lost the realization of emptiness.

It has already been explained that because the worldly dharmas—the defilements of adventitious stains—and the supramundane dharmakāya, which possesses the qualities of the naturally pure emptiness of intrinsic nature, are inseparable, it receives its name [dharmakāya].
What does this clarify?

Furthermore, by means of the gate of non-discriminative wisdom regarding the dharma-realm of single flavor and equal flavor, one contemplates the supramundane dharmakāya that is pure by nature; this is called knowing and seeing suchness as it truly is.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes can see the Tathāgatagarbha only in a small measure; how much more so for ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and others.
Thus, the verse says:
Just as when thin clouds part, one sees the sun in the sky,
so do the sages of pure wisdom perceive the Buddha.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are like those who lack eyesight.
One cannot perceive the Tathāgata, Like a blind person who does not see the sun.
All phenomena that can be known Are immeasurable and boundless;
Pervading the entire dharma-realm of space, Only infinite wisdom can perceive them.
The Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas pervades all places;
the Buddha’s wisdom is able to see it because of its immeasurable knowledge.
Chapter Seven: On the Purpose for Teaching. In the *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra*, Chapter Seven: On the Purpose for Teaching. Question: [What is the purpose for teaching?]

The meaning of *tathatā*, *buddhadhātu*, and *tathāgatagarbha* is not even within the sphere of the foremost sages—bodhisattvas dwelling on the ultimate bodhisattva stages who are free from all obstructions—because it is the sphere of the Omniscient One alone.
If this is so, for what reason was it taught to foolish, deluded, and ordinary worldlings?
The answer is:
For this reason, four verses are briefly stated:
In various sūtras it is taught that all things, internal and external, are empty;
that conditioned phenomena are like clouds, and like dreams, illusions, and so forth.
Why, then, is it said here that all sentient beings—
All possess the nature of the Tathāgata, yet why do you not speak of emptiness and quiescence?
Because they harbor hearts of cowardice, they treat all sentient beings with contempt;
clinging to illusory dharmas, they slander true suchness and the Buddha-nature.
One calculates that there is a divine self within the body.
In order to cause those who hold such views to distance themselves from these five kinds of faults, it is said that there is Buddha-nature.
It should be understood that these four lines of verse are briefly explained by means of eleven verses.
The verse says:
Within all the sūtras, it is taught that all conditioned phenomena—
namely afflictions, karma, and so forth— are as false as clouds and the like.
Afflictions are like clouds; the karma one performs is like a dream.
The aggregates (skandhas) are likewise like illusions, for they arise from afflictions and karma.
This has already been stated previously in this ultimate treatise.
To avoid five kinds of faults, it is taught that the nature of *tathatā* exists.
Because sentient beings do not hear this, they fail to resolve upon bodhicitta;
or else, with hearts of cowardice, they commit the fault of deceiving themselves.
Before having generated the bodhicitta, one gives rise to thoughts of deceit and arrogance;
seeing one who has generated the bodhicitta, one thinks, "I am superior to that bodhisattva.
Such a person of pride does not give rise to a mind of right wisdom.
Therefore, through false grasping, one does not know the reality of things as they are.
One falsely grasps at the faults of sentient beings, failing to realize that these are adventitious defilements of the mind;
in truth, those faults do not exist, for the nature of reality is pure and endowed with merit.
Because they grasp at false errors and do not know true merit,
they are unable to give rise to the compassion that views self and others as equal.
Hearing of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), they arouse great heroic power.
And by revering the World-Honored One, wisdom, and great compassion,
one gives rise to and increases five dharmas: non-retrogression and equanimity,
being free from all faults, and possessing only all virtues.
Regarding all sentient beings, As being no different from my own body, They shall swiftly achieve accomplishment Of unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment. Chapter Eight:

The Transformation of the Body into Purity and the Attainment of Bodhi. *Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, Chapter Eight: "The Transformation of the Body into Purity and the Attainment of Bodhi. The Treatise states:
Having already explained the *tathatā* with stains, from this point forward, one should know that the stainless *tathatā* is being explained.

Regarding the stainless *tathatā*: it refers to how all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, within the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma-realm, remain far removed from all various kinds of defilements; they transform their coarse and impure bodies to attain pure and wondrous bodies. One should know that the nature of true suchness, the untainted Dharma-body, is briefly explained through eight categories of meaning.
What are these eight?
The verse says:
Purity, attainment, and distancing; being conjoined with the benefit of oneself and others.
Relying on the profound, the swift, and the great, with temporal duration corresponding to those dharmas—
this is called the sequence of the eightfold meaning of the phrases.
Regarding the single verse that manifests these eight meanings, what are the eight?
First, substantial entity; second, cause; third, fruit; fourth, activity; fifth, association; sixth, practice; seventh, permanence; eighth, inconceivability.

Regarding the "substantial entity": it should be understood that what was previously described as the *tathāgatagarbha*—which is not separate from being enveloped by the sheath of afflictions—is, upon the removal of all afflictions and the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), attained in its purity; this is what is called the substantial entity.
The verse says:
"Because it is pure.
Therefore, the *Ārya-Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
World-Honored One!

If one has no doubt regarding the tathāgatagarbha that is enveloped by immeasurable stores of afflictions, then one likewise has no doubt regarding the dharmakāya that emerges from those immeasurable stores of afflictions.
As for the cause, there are two kinds of non-conceptual wisdom:

first, supramundane non-conceptual wisdom; second, the wisdom of practice based on both the mundane and the supramundane, which is attained by relying on supramundane wisdom. These are called the cause.
The verse says:
"Because it is attained.
As for the fruit:
Based on this very attainment, one realizes the fruit of realized knowledge; this is what is called the "fruit.
As the verse says:
"Because of being far removed."
As for "practice" (yoga), there are two kinds of distancing:
first, distancing from the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa); second, distancing from the obstacle to knowledge (jñeyāvaraṇa). It is called "distancing" according to this sequence.
Thus, being free from [the duality of] self-benefit and benefit for others constitutes accomplishment; this is called "activity.
The verse says:
"Because it benefits both self and others."

Regarding "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*): it refers to attaining immeasurable merit through benefiting oneself and others, and abiding in this state eternally and ultimately; this is called correspondence.
As the verse says:
"Because of correspondence."

Regarding "the constant and inconceivable activity," this refers to the three kinds of Buddha-dharmakāya; from beginningless worlds until now, they constantly and without rest perform the benefit of sentient beings, which is inconceivable.
The verse says:
"Because it relies upon that which is profound, swift, and great.
For this reason, the verse is stated in brief:
The substantial cause, the result, and the activity, As well as the associated formations, Are eternally inconceivable; Know this to be named the Buddha-ground.
Furthermore, based on the substantial entity, based on the cause within the Buddha-ground, and because of attaining the causal means for that, three verses are spoken:
As previously explained, the Buddha’s Dharma-body is a naturally pure essence that is defiled by the adventitious stains of the various afflictions.
It is like the sun and moon in the sky, which are pure and free from impurity.
Enveloped by that thick and dense cloud, And covered by a net of obscurations,
The Buddha’s merit is stainless, Eternal, constant, and unchanging.
Without discriminating among phenomena, He has attained untainted, true wisdom.
These three verses should be understood as being briefly explained by the following four verses.
The verses say:
The Buddha’s body never abandons The pure, true, and wondrous Dharma.
Like the sun and moon in the sky, wisdom is free from defilement and non-dual.
The qualities of the Buddha-dharma, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— luminous and pure—
are associated with that which is not produced by conditions, yet they do not depart from its essential reality.
The afflictions and the cognitive obstructions—these phenomena lack any real essence;
they are constantly defiled by adventitious dust, and for this reason they are likened to clouds.
Having distanced themselves from these two causes, they proceed toward the non-conceptuality of the two [natures].
"Non-conceptual true wisdom, and that which is attained based upon it.
What does this verse clarify?
It clarifies that the aforementioned transformation of the basis is, in its essential nature, pure.
Furthermore, purity is briefly of two kinds.
What are these two?
First is natural purity; second is purity through the removal of defilements.

Regarding "purity by nature": it refers to liberation by nature, which involves no relinquishing or abandoning. This is because the essence of that naturally pure mind does not abandon any adventitious afflictions, for they have never been associated with it from the very beginning.
That which is "stainless and pure" refers to the attainment of liberation.

Furthermore, that liberation is not separate from all phenomena; it is like water being called "pure" despite its inseparability from various sediments and impurities. This is because the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) is free from the adventitious stains of afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa-mala*), with nothing remaining beyond this.
Furthermore, based on the purity resulting from the removal of defilements in that fruit, four verses are spoken:
Like the waters of a pure pond, Free from all turbidity and silt,
Surrounded on all sides By various kinds of flowering trees.
Like the moon released from Rāhu, or the sun free from the veil of clouds, the body manifests as the very essence endowed with stainless qualities.
It is like the honey of the king of bees, rich in flavor; it is like solid, pure, and genuine gold.
The great fruit-bearing tree of the treasure-store, The stainless image of pure gold,
The body of a wheel-turning sage king, And the image of the Tathāgata of wondrous jewels—
All such dharmas as these Are themselves the body of the Tathāgata.
These four lines of verse should be understood through a brief explanation in eight lines of verse.
The verse says:
The adventitious afflictions such as greed Are like turbidity and dust in water.
Non-conceptual supreme wisdom is like the water in a pond;
it manifests the Buddha’s Dharma-body and all its merits.
Because these depend upon the fruit of realized gnosis, it is described in this way.
Greed is like turbid water and dust; when pure dharmas are mixed with defilements, sentient beings can be transformed like lotus flowers surrounding a pond.
Moistened by the habitual energy of meditative concentration, they remain far removed from the Rāhu of anger.
With the water of great compassion, he benefits all sentient beings everywhere.
Like the moon on the fifteenth day, freed from the net of clouds,
his radiance shines upon sentient beings and can dispel all deep darkness.
The Buddha is a stainless sun and moon; having parted from the net-like clouds of delusion, his light of wisdom illuminates sentient beings and extinguishes all darkness.
Having attained the peerless Dharma, he is able to bestow the flavor of the sublime Dharma.
The Buddhas are like the core of honey, Far removed from the obstacles of bees and husks.
Possessing true and wondrous merit, They eliminate all forms of poverty;
Able to bestow the power of liberation, They are thus likened to the golden tree.
The Dharma Jewel is the true body; it is the supreme among two-legged beings, and its excellent form is ultimately perfected. Therefore, the latter three similes are taught.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that by means of two kinds of wisdom, one relies upon the activities of benefiting oneself and others.
What are these two? First, supramundane non-conceptual wisdom;
second, the transformation of the basis by relying on supramundane non-conceptual wisdom, whereby one attains a body whose activity is free from afflictions and realizes the fruit of realized wisdom.
Furthermore, what is the accomplishment of one's own benefit?

It refers to attaining liberation, being far removed from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and far removed from the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and attaining the unobstructed, pure *dharmakāya*; this is called accomplishing the benefit of oneself.
Furthermore, what constitutes the accomplishment of the benefit of others?

Having already accomplished one’s own benefit, one spontaneously manifests in the world through the power of sovereign action by means of those two kinds of Buddha-bodies, based upon [the former] from time immemorial; this is called the accomplishment of the benefit of others.
Furthermore, based on the meaning of accomplishing the activities of benefiting oneself and others,
four verses are spoken: Untainted and all-pervading, Unceasing, eternal, Cool, immutable,
And the non-retrogressive, quiescent, and pure state.
The bodies of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are like space, devoid of marks;
yet for the sake of those of supreme wisdom, they serve as the objects of the six sense faculties.
They manifest subtle and wondrous forms and produce sublime sounds.
Causing them to smell the fragrance of the Buddha’s precepts, And granting them the flavor of the Buddha’s sublime Dharma;
Causing them to awaken to the touch of samādhi, And leading them to know the profound and wondrous Dharma.
Through subtle contemplation of the dense forest [of phenomena], The Buddha is seen as free from the marks of empty space.
These four lines of verse should be understood as being briefly explained by the following eight lines of verse:
"In brief, two kinds of phenomena— Action and wisdom— should be known."
The body of liberation is fulfilled, the pure and true Dharma-body;
one should know that these two—the body of liberation and the Dharma-body—are also one, namely:
the untainted, the all-pervading, and the ultimate unconditioned.
Because afflictions are exhausted and outflows are absent, and because habitual tendencies have been extinguished,
one should know that wisdom is all-pervading, being both unimpeded and free from obstruction.
It is unconditioned because it does not perish, for its essential substance is never lost.
Non-loss is called the root; it is explained by the phrases beginning with "constant.
Regarding these phrases beginning with "constant," one should know there are four types of loss:
death, impermanence, transformation, and inconceivable retrogression.
Because it is deathless, it is eternal; because it is eternal, it is cool;
because it does not revolve, it is unchanging; because it is tranquil, it does not regress.
That ultimate footprint is the essence of pure wisdom and the white dharmas.
Fully endowed with forms, sounds, and so forth, they manifest through the various sense faculties.
Just as space is without characteristics yet manifests the characteristics of form and the rest, so too is the Dharma-body:
it possesses the spheres of the six sense faculties.
What does this verse clarify?

When it is stated in the sūtras that "the Buddhas are likewise like the nature of space," this is said with reference to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), based on the unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of the pure *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Thus it is spoken.
For this reason, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of the thirty-two marks of a great man?
Subhūti replied,
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one does not see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks."
The Buddha said: "So it is,
so it is, Subhūti!"
One does not see the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of physical marks, Subhūti!

If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of physical marks, then a Wheel-turning Sage King would be a Tathāgata; therefore, it is not by means of the perfection of physical marks that one sees the Tathāgata.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies this meaning by relying upon the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the pure Dharma-body (dharma-kāya).
Furthermore, based on the sense of "correspondence" (yoga), two verses are spoken:
Like space, it is inconceivable, eternal, and perpetually cool;
it is unchanging and quiescent, universally free from all conceptualization.
It is unattached in all places, and free from obstructive or coarse sensations.
Nor can it be grasped through views; the Buddha’s pure mind is free from defilement.
These two lines of verse should be understood as being briefly explained by the following eight lines of verse:
[The verses follow:]
The liberation body and the dharma body demonstrate self-benefit and benefit for others;
based upon self-benefit and benefit for others,
the meaning of their correspondence therein should be known as all inconceivable merits.
Because it is not the object of the three types of wisdom, it is known by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Buddha-nature of all sentient beings is subtle; therefore, it is not the object of hearing, nor is it the object of the first [wisdom], which is reflection.
The world’s practitioners of wisdom do not know it;
all deluded ordinary beings have never seen it from the beginning, like the blind who do not behold forms.
Those of the Two Vehicles are like infants, unable to see the orbs of the sun and moon.
Because it is unarisen, it is eternal; because it is undestroyed, it is constant.
Because it is free from duality, it is cool; because the nature of phenomena abides without change, it is unchanging.
Because it realizes cessation, it is quiescent; because it awakens to all things, it is pervasive.
Abiding nowhere and free from conceptualization, detached from afflictions and unattached;
with no obstruction from the veil of ignorance and free from hindrance, supple and free from coarseness.
Formless and invisible, free from marks and ungraspable.
"Pure by virtue of its intrinsic nature, Stainless because it is free from defilement.
What does this verse clarify?
The analogy of space clarifies that the unconditioned virtues of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are not separate from the Buddha-dharmakāya.

It should be understood that for all states of existence, he attains inconceivable, supreme, and great activities of skillful means, supreme activities of great compassion, and supreme activities of great wisdom; and for the sake of bestowing upon all sentient beings the three types of Buddha-bodies—namely, the Essential Buddha (*dharmakāya*), the Buddha who enjoys the Dharma (*sambhogakāya*), and the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*)—which are characterized by bliss, stainlessness, and purity, he constantly practices without rest and without interruption, spontaneously, for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Because it is not shared with others, but is associated exclusively with the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies that because the various distinctions of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are associated with this body, eight verses are spoken:
Neither beginning, middle, nor end; unbroken and non-dual;
far removed from the three realms, stainless and free from conceptual discrimination—this profound sphere is not known by those of the two vehicles.
One who possesses supreme samādhi and wisdom, such a person is able to see the inconceivable merits that exceed the sands of the Ganges;
these are achieved only by the Tathāgata and are not shared with others.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body, A pure and stainless essence,
Is far removed from all afflictions And all habitual tendencies.
With various supreme and wondrous dharmas, It takes radiance as its very substance.
Causing sentient beings to attain liberation, It is ever without rest.
Its activities are inconceivable, Like the king of maṇi jewels,
which can manifest various forms, Yet its essence is not real.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of the world, manifesting the state of tranquility;
he teaches and transforms beings until they are matured, bestowing predictions of enlightenment to lead them into the Way.
The Tathāgata’s body is like a reflected image, yet it does not depart from its original essence.
Just as all forms are never separate from space,
these eight lines of verse should be understood through a brief explanation in twenty-five verses.
The verses say:
As previously explained, the Buddha’s Dharma-body, as well as omniscience,
mastery, and nirvana, the ultimate truth, inconceivable dharmas,
and the qualities such as those of the Arhat— these are [the attributes of the Tathāgata].
To be personally realized within oneself—this is how one should understand it.
Those distinctions of the three bodies—the real, the enjoyment, and the emanation—are what are called the profound, the swift, and the great: the body of immeasurable merit.
To clarify the body of the true essence: it refers to the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, which, briefly stated, has five characteristics; its five virtues should be known.
It is unconditioned and undifferentiated, and it is far removed from the two extremes.
Having emerged from the afflictive obscurations, The cognitive obscurations, and the obscurations to samādhi;
Because all stains have been abandoned, It is the domain of the noble ones,
Illuminated by pure radiance, For such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Immeasurable and incalculable, beyond thought and comparison,
With all such peerless merits, he has reached the supreme shore.
In accord with the true Dharma-body, his bliss is truly beyond counting.
Beyond the realm of discursive thought, and far removed from habitual tendencies;
the boundless and equal Buddha-dharmas, in their sequence, never depart from the retributive body.
Experiencing the various flavors of the Dharma, they manifest all manner of wondrous forms.
Having purified the habitual tendencies of compassion, free from false conceptualization,
they benefit all sentient beings spontaneously and without ceasing.
Like a wish-fulfilling jewel, they satisfy the hearts of sentient beings.
The Buddha who experiences bliss is thus, with sovereign power through his supernormal faculties.
This sovereignty of power is briefly said to be of five kinds:
preaching the Dharma, being visible, and the uninterrupted performance of all activities.
As well as resting and vanishing, manifesting non-substantial entities—
this is called the brief explanation of the five kinds of mastery.
Like a mani jewel, depending upon various colors,
The various marks of other birth-stories are all unreal;
the Tathāgata is likewise, manifesting through the power of skillful means:
descending from Tuṣita, he enters the womb and is born in due succession.
He practiced and mastered all arts; as an infant, he entered the royal palace.
Disgusted by the marks of all desires, he left the home life to practice austerities.
He questioned various non-Buddhist teachers and then proceeded to the site of enlightenment.
Having subdued the hosts of Māras, he attained the rank of the Great and Wondrously Awakened Honored One;
he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and entered *nirvāṇa* without remainder,
manifesting such deeds as these within impure lands.
Without ceasing in this world, he proclaims the names of impermanence,
suffering, non-self, and tranquility; through the power of his skillful means and wisdom,
he causes all those sentient beings to feel weary of and detached from the suffering of the three realms.
Later, they enter into nirvana, having entered the path of tranquility.
Yet those śrāvakas possess this false appearance,
saying, "I have attained nirvana."
All preach the Dharma as it truly is, encompassed by wisdom and skillful means;
they turn back the former deluded mind, causing it to mature in the Supreme Vehicle,
and bestow the prediction of wondrous Bodhi.
Subtle, of great power, and causing foolish sentient beings to pass beyond the perilous and evil paths—these should be understood as being taught in sequence: profound, swift, and great.
The first is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, the second is the Rūpakāya Buddha;
just as all physical forms exist within the void of space,
so too does the final body exist within the body of the first Buddha.
From this point onward, based upon these three kinds of Buddha-bodies, for the sake of bringing joy to sentient beings and benefiting sentient beings,
two verses are briefly stated:
The essence of the World-Honored One is eternally abiding, Because he has cultivated immeasurable causes.
The realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible;
With a compassionate mind as vast as space, wisdom is perfected in accord with reality.
Attaining mastery within the Dharma, one subdues all maras and adversaries; Because its essence is quiescent, it is eternal.
These two verses should be understood as being briefly explained by the following six verses.
The verses say:
"Abandoning body, life, and wealth, One gathers all the Buddha-dharmas."
For the benefit of sentient beings, you have ultimately fulfilled your original vow.
Having attained the pure Buddha-body and giving rise to great compassion,
you practice the four bases of psychic power and abide in the world by their power.
Having accomplished sublime wisdom, they have abandoned the mind that seeks nirvāṇa within existence;
always attaining samādhi of the mind, they achieve union with bliss.
Constantly remaining in the world, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Having attained the state of pure nectar, one is thus free from all Māras.
Since the Buddhas are fundamentally unarisen and primordially quiescent, they are eternally worthy of refuge; therefore, it is said: "I take refuge."
The first seven similes illustrate the permanence of the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya);
the latter three similes illustrate the permanence of the Sugata’s dharma-body (dharmakāya).
What meaning does this verse clarify?
It should be known that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, by relying on the dharma-body, attain the unsurpassed body;
this is inconceivable. Because it is inconceivable, two verses are spoken:
"It is not something expressed by words, It is subsumed within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
Transcending the stages of vitarka and vicāra, it is beyond all analogy and cannot be described.
This most supreme and wondrous Dharma does not grasp at existence or nirvāṇa;
it is not known by those of the three vehicles, but is solely the realm of the Buddha.
These two verses should be understood as being briefly explained by the following five verses.
The verses say:
"Inconceivable and ungraspable, Because it is free from the characteristics of language."
That which is free from the characteristics of language is subsumed by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
That which is subsumed by the ultimate truth is not the domain of discursive thought;
that which is not the domain of discursive thought is known through the absence of analogy.
One who knows through the absence of analogy, by means of the most supreme and unsurpassed;
that which is most supreme and unsurpassed does not grasp at existence or nirvana.
Not grasping at these two, one does not grasp at virtues or faults.
The first five similes represent permanence that is subtle and inconceivable;
the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternal. As for the sixth simile, because he has attained mastery, the Tathāgata’s form-body is eternal.
Chapter Nine: The Qualities of the Tathāgata. The *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra* states:

Having already explained the stainless *dharmakāya* of suchness, we shall next explain all the qualities that depend upon that stainless *dharmakāya* of suchness. Just as a *maṇi* jewel is not separate from its radiance, color, and various characteristics, so too are the immeasurable and boundless qualities of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya*—which are intrinsically pure and stainless.
For this reason, following the qualities of the Buddha, two verses are spoken:
Benefiting oneself as well as others, The body of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
Depending upon that body of true reality, There exists this body of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The fruit is the state of being far removed and fully matured;
within this, there are sixty-four kinds of dharmas, which are the various distinctions of all meritorious qualities.
What meaning does this verse demonstrate?
The verse says:
Because one achieves [realization] within oneself and sustains all Buddha-dharmas,
one gathers the first body (svābhāvika-kāya) to sustain the bodies of others.
Because all Tathāgatas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the substance of conventional truth,
one should know that the immeasurable merits of the Buddha are subsumed within the first body (the *nirmāṇakāya*).
These include the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*).
"That which experiences the retribution of bliss is subsumed within the second Buddha-body.
What does this verse clarify?
It clarifies the sixty-four kinds of meritorious qualities of the Buddha-body, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*).
How is this known?
Based on that meaning, two verses are briefly stated:
The vajra-pestle of the Buddha’s power Shatters the obstructions of those lacking wisdom.
The Tathāgata is fearless, dwelling among the assembly like a lion;
the unique qualities of the Tathāgata are as pure as space.
Like the moon reflected in water, sentient beings perceive them in two ways.

From this point onward, the remaining verses of the *Guṇavarga* (Chapter on Qualities) sequentially demonstrate those sixty-four kinds of Tathāgata qualities, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), as extensively explained in the *Dhāraṇīśvararāja-sūtra*; these should be understood accordingly.
First, based on the ten powers (*daśabala*), two verses are spoken: The possible and the impossible,
the ripening of fruits, Karma and the various faculties,
The nature [of beings], inclinations, the paths leading everywhere, And the stainless meditative concentrations.
"Recalling past lives, the tranquil wisdom of the divine eye"—
such verses as these declare the names of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Furthermore, based on the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), three verses are spoken:
To realize all phenomena as they truly are, to eliminate the obstacles of the hindering paths,
and to teach the path that attains the outflow-free state— these are the four kinds of fearlessness.
Regarding the objects of knowledge, he possesses ultimate knowledge of both himself and others.
Knowing for oneself and teaching others to know—this does not obstruct the path.
It is able to realize the supreme and wondrous fruit; having attained it oneself, one enables others to attain it as well.
Teaching the truths of self-benefit and benefit for others—this is fearlessness in all circumstances.
Furthermore, based on the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), eight verses are spoken:
The Buddha has no faults and no contention; He is free from errors such as false recollection;
He has no unconcentrated or distracted mind; He has no manifold perceptions.
Without mental effort, he guards his mind; with desire and diligence, he does not retreat.
In mindfulness, wisdom, and liberation, as well as in knowledge and vision, he does not regress.
All karmas have wisdom as their root; he knows the three periods of time without obstruction.
The eighteen qualities of a Buddha, as well as those not yet mentioned:
the Buddha’s body and speech are without fault;
even if others come to cause destruction, his inner mind shows no sign of agitation, nor does he harbor thoughts of malice or indifference.
The World-Honored One’s desire, diligence, and energy, his pure mindfulness, wisdom, and liberation, and his knowledge and vision never falter; he manifests the realm that can be known.
All various karmas and the like proceed with wisdom as their fundamental basis.
Unimpeded throughout the three periods of time, The vast practice of wisdom is ever-present.
This is called the essence of the Tathāgata, In accord with great wisdom;
Awakening to that great bodhi, The most supreme and wondrous Dharma.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he turns the great wheel of Dharma—
the fearless, supreme, and wondrous teaching— enabling them to attain liberation. Furthermore,
based upon the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, eleven verses are spoken:
Your feet are level and full, complete with thousand-spoked wheels;
your heels are high and your insteps are elevated; your calves are like those of the eneya deer king;
your hands and feet are entirely soft and supple, and all your fingers are slender and long.
The King of Geese has webbed fingers; his upper and lower arms are well-rounded;
his two shoulders are level from front to back; both sides are perfectly symmetrical;
standing, his hands reach below his knees; he possesses the horse-king’s characteristic of the concealed organ.
His body is well-proportioned and grand, like the king of *nyagrodha* trees;
his physical form is full in seven places, and the upper half of his body is like that of a lion.
His majestic power is firm and stable, just like that of Nārāyaṇa.
The color of his body is fresh, pure, and exquisite; his skin is soft and golden-hued.
It is clean, supple, fine, even, and dense, with a single hair growing from each pore.
These hairs are soft, curling upward, subtle, and turn to the right like wheels.
The body’s pure radiance is perfectly circular, The mark upon the crown of the head is lofty and prominent;
The nape of the neck is like that of the king of peacocks, And the jaw is square like that of a lion.
The hair is as pure as the color of refined gold, Comparable to that of Indra.
The white tuft of hair between the eyebrows emits a pure radiance that illuminates the entire face;
his mouth contains forty teeth, two of which are as white as snow, deep and closely set yet luminous within and without;
the upper and lower rows of teeth are perfectly even and aligned.
With a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, a wondrous sound deep and far-reaching;
whatever he eats appears at his throat, obtaining the supreme flavor among all flavors;
with a tongue that is slender, thin, broad, and long; and with two eyes of a pure, deep blue color.
His glances are like those of a bull-king; his merit is like that of a lotus flower.
Thus the Honored One among Men is described as possessing the thirty-two sublime marks, each distinct and unconfused, such that no part of his entire body is to be disparaged.

These ten powers of a Buddha, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, and thirty-two marks of a great man, when briefly gathered together in one place, should be known as the sixty-four kinds of merit.
The verse says:
Regarding the sixty-four virtues, both the cultivated causes and their resultant rewards are each distinct;
these are explained in sequence in the Jewel Sūtra.
What does this verse clarify?

It clarifies that the distinctions between the causes and fruits of the sixty-four kinds of merits of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as previously explained, should be understood as they are extensively taught in the *Ratnadattā-sūtra* according to this sequence.
Furthermore, based on these four points, there are four successive metaphors—namely, the vajra, the lion king, the analogy of space, and the moon in water—expressed in nine lines of verse.
Based on those nine verses, the summary is stated in verse:
Violating [the precepts] and lacking a compassionate heart, Not sharing [merit] and being devoid of intention—
Therefore, the mallet and the lion, And the metaphors of the moon in the sky and in water are taught.
Furthermore, based on the analogy of the vajra of the ten powers, two verses are spoken:
The nature of what is possible and impossible, the fruits, The various faculties of faith of sentient beings,
The various paths, stages of cultivation, And the distinctions of past lives.
The divine eye, the exhaustion of outflows, and so forth— these are the vajra-hammers of the Buddha’s power,
capable of piercing, shattering, dispersing, and cleaving the armor of ignorance, the mountains, walls, and trees.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
To state it briefly in verse:
The six powers of all Tathāgatas— The second, third, and first, respectively—
Within the sphere of the objects of knowledge, Are free from the obstacles to samādhi.
And having abandoned other defilements and hindrances—
just as when armor, walls, trees, and the like are shattered, scattered, or cut, though they may be heavy and solid,
they can no longer be destroyed.
The ten powers of the Tathāgata are like that vajra; therefore, they are called the "vajra-pestle.
Furthermore, based on the analogy of the lion king regarding the four fearlessnesses, two verses are spoken:
Just as the lion king is sovereign among all beasts,
Dwelling constantly in the mountain forests, Without fear of any wild animals;
So too is the Buddha, the King of Men, Abiding amidst the multitudes.
"Fearlessness and firm abiding, Steadfastness, vigor, and so forth.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
To state it briefly in verse:
Knowing the suffering of illness and its cause,
he taught the noble path as the wondrous medicine to distance oneself from that cause of suffering and realize cessation.
Having distanced himself from all fears, he dwells well within the city of *Vikrānta*.
The Buddha-King amidst the great assembly is fearless like a lion;
because he knows all dharmas, he is able to dwell securely and is without fear in any place.
The two vehicles and those who are purified, seeing that I have no equal,
maintain minds that are always concentrated and firm amidst all phenomena.
For what reason is he named "The Swift One" (Vikrāmin)?
Having transcended the ground of the dwelling of ignorance and abiding in the state of sovereign unimpededness, it is therefore called "the Vigorous Stride" (*vikrīḍita*).
Furthermore, based on the analogy of space regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), three verses are spoken:
Earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth— Those phenomena do not exist within space.
Within all forms there is also none; space is the unobstructed dharma.
All Buddhas are without obstruction, possessing characteristics like empty space.
When the Tathāgata dwells in the world, he is like earth, water, fire, and wind.
Yet all the merits possessed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
do not share even a single dharma with anything else in the world.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
To summarize, it is said in verse:
For the sake of the śrāvakas and the vidyādharas, For the wise and those who have attained mastery,
And for the sake of the increasingly subtle dharmas, The five great elements are thus manifested.
All sentient beings enjoy it, Like earth, water, fire, and wind;
Transcending both the mundane and the supramundane, It is therefore called the Great Space.
Possessing thirty-two virtues, It exists in reliance upon the Dharmakāya.
Just as the wick of a worldly lamp, its light, warmth, and form,
are inseparable and without distinction;
so too are the Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas and all their merits without distinction.
Furthermore, based on the analogy of the moon in the water regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, two verses are spoken:
When the autumn sky is free from the obscuration of clouds, The moon appears in both the heavens and the water;
All people throughout the world Behold the power of the moon.
Within the pure wheel of the Buddha, endowed with the power of merit, the Son of the Buddha beholds the Tathāgata; his body of merit is likewise so.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
To summarize in verse:
The thirty-two marks of merit, Which bring joy to those who behold them, Exist as three kinds of Buddhas:
The Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.
The Dharma-body is pure and stainless, Transcending the mundane world;
While situated within the wheel of the Tathāgata, Sentient beings perceive it in two places.
Just as when one sees the reflection of the moon In clear, pure water,
These thirty-two marks are named in dependence upon the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Just as a mani-jewel is never separate from its radiant colors and marks,
so too is the form-body never separate from the thirty-two marks.
Chapter Ten: The Spontaneous and Uninterrupted Buddha-Activities. The *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra* states:
Having already explained the stainless qualities of the Buddhas, we shall now explain the activities performed by the Tathāgatas.
One should know that the activities of those Buddhas proceed spontaneously and are constantly uninterrupted in their teaching and transformation of sentient beings.
It should be understood that, based on this brief explanation, there are two kinds of dharmas that proceed spontaneously.
For this reason, because the activities of all Buddhas proceed spontaneously, never ceasing and always performing the work of a Buddha, six verses are spoken:
Regarding those sentient beings who are ready to be transformed, By means of skillful methods of transformation,
They initiate the activity of transforming sentient beings, Thus transforming the realms of sentient beings.
The Buddhas, masters of sovereignty, for those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed,
always await the proper place and the proper time, spontaneously performing the work of a Buddha.
They possess the universal realization of the Mahāyāna, the most wondrous accumulation of merit.
Like the waters and jewels of the great ocean, so too is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Awakening is vast and boundless, like the realm of empty space;
amidst immeasurable merits, it is the sunlight of great wisdom.
Universally illuminating all sentient beings, there is the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma-body, a treasury of stainless merit; it is no different from my own body.
Enveloped by the nets of clouds and mist—the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations— [it remains hidden].
The winds of the Buddhas’ compassion blow them away until they are utterly extinguished.
The meaning of these six lines of verse should be understood through a brief explanation in fourteen verses,
which state:
By means of the wisdom of what nature, at what time, and in what place, does one perform actions without discrimination? Therefore, karma is spontaneous.
By means of what faculties and natures can sentient beings be liberated?
By what kind of wisdom can one deliver all sentient beings?
Furthermore, what constitutes the skillful means for transforming sentient beings?
In what place and at what time may sentient beings be transformed?
Progression and merit, The fruit and its gathering, Its obstacles and the severing of those obstacles— These various conditions are not to be discriminated.
"Progression" refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*); "Merit" has the two truths as its cause.
The fruit is called Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi), which encompasses the retinue of enlightenment.
Its obstacles are said to be boundless: the afflictions (kleśa) along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā).
The severing of these obstacles consists of great loving-kindness (maitrī), great compassion (karuṇā), and so forth.
These are called the six sense bases, which at all times and through various causes and conditions, are explained in this sequence; one should understand them thus.
They are like the waters, jewels, sky, sun, earth, clouds, and wind of the great ocean.
The stages are like a great ocean, with the waters of wisdom and the jewels of merit;
enlightenment is like the realm of space, vast and without middle or end.
To benefit sentient beings, the two kinds of activity are like the sun.
He is able to universally and completely perceive that within the realms of all sentient beings there exists the nature of the Tathāgata, like a treasure hidden beneath the earth.
Just as that great earth is in its essence stable and immovable, so too is this nature.
For the benefit of sentient beings, one perceives that self and others are no different.
Adventitious afflictions and the like are from the beginning devoid of intrinsic nature;
all are utterly illusory, like a gathering of clouds lacking reality.
Arousing great compassion, like a fierce wind blowing,
the afflictions and cognitive obstructions are exhausted, like clouds gathering and dispersing.
Because the work of transformation is not yet complete, they remain forever in the world.
From the very beginningless limit, it has been spontaneous and uninterrupted. Question:

As previously stated, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are neither born nor extinguished; if this is so, they are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and that which is an unconditioned phenomenon does not engage in the cultivation of karmic actions.
What is the spontaneous, uninterrupted, and constant activity of teaching and transforming sentient beings?
The answer is:
in order to manifest those great deeds of the Buddhas that sever all doubts and delusions, one relies upon those inconceivable, stainless, and pure Buddha-realms to manifest these great deeds.
Therefore, it is explained by means of a single verse of analogy:
The drum of Śakra, the cloud, Brahmā, the sun, and the maṇi jewel, The echo,
as well as space and the earth— The body of the Tathāgata is likewise.
Based on the meaning condensed in this single line of the sūtra, nine types of similes are presented in verse.
From here onwards, it should be understood that the remaining sixty-six verses provide a detailed exposition.
Furthermore, based on the meaning of those verses explained in detail, their significance is summarized through nine similes.
Moreover, it should be understood that the ultimate cultivation for the unsurpassed benefit of all sentient beings by the Tathāgata is explained in detail in successive order through nineteen verses.
The verse says:
Having distanced oneself from all karma, one has never seen its fruit;
for the sake of all those who doubt, it removes the net of their various uncertainties.
Nine kinds of similes are taught; that sūtra’s name extensively explains these various dharmas.
Within that sūtra, nine similes are explained at length; it is named the "Sphere of Wisdom."
Adorned with swift and wondrous wisdom, the wise enter quickly and become fully endowed with the realm of the Buddhas.
Like a beryl mirror-image and so forth— these are the nine kinds of similes.
One should know its essential meaning through seeing, teaching, and universal presence.
By means of wisdom that is free from all signs, the secrets of body, speech,
and mind are attained by the Great Compassionate One, who is devoid of any effortful mental activity.
Non-conceptual and tranquil, stainless by virtue of wisdom,
like great lapis lazuli, with Indra and others as metaphors;
because wisdom is ultimately fulfilled, it is ultimately tranquil.
Because there is pure wisdom, there is no conceptual differentiation.
To establish various meanings, similes such as "explanation" (vyākhyāna) and so forth are taught;
to establish those meanings, the nine kinds of views and so forth are taught.
Detached from birth and detached from supernatural powers, the Buddhas manifest these matters;
this is called a brief explanation through various meanings and parables.
First, a parable is used to explain what differs from the latter; later, a parable is used to explain what differs from the former.
The Buddha’s body is like a reflected image, Like that lapis lazuli ground.
It is not that people do not have voices, Like the wondrous Dharma drum of the heavens;
It is not that it does not perform the work of the Dharma, Like that great rain from the clouds.
It is not that it does not bring benefit,
nor is it that it does not give rise to the various kinds of seeds, remaining as immovable as Brahmā;
yet it is not that it does not bring them to full maturity, like that great solar orb.
It is not that it does not dispel all darkness, like that wish-fulfilling gem;
yet it is not that it is not rare, like that echo;
it is not that it is not produced through causes and conditions, like that space.
It is not that he does not act for the sake of all; He serves as a refuge for sentient beings, just like the great earth, Which does not fail to support all manner of things;
For it is by depending upon that great earth [that they abide].
Because they bear the weight of all worlds and their manifold things;
by relying on the bodhi of all Buddhas, the sublime Dharma that transcends the world,
they accomplish all pure deeds, the various dhyānas, and the four immeasurables.
And through the four formless absorptions, the Tathāgatas, acting spontaneously,
eternally abide throughout all worlds; possessing such karmic activities,
they perform these wondrous deeds simultaneously, without succession.
Chapter Eleven: Comparing the Merit of Faith. *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra Śāstra*. The treatise states:
Having previously explained the four kinds of dharmas, from this point onward it clarifies how a person of wisdom can give rise to faith toward those dharmas.
Regarding the merit obtained by those who rely on that faith, fourteen verses are spoken:
The Buddha-nature, the Buddha’s enlightenment, The Buddha’s Dharma, and the Buddha’s deeds—
These cannot be conceived By any pure beings of the world.
If there are those who can have faith in this realm of all Buddhas,
they shall obtain immeasurable merit, surpassing all sentient beings.
By seeking the Bodhi of the Buddha, they will attain inconceivable karmic rewards.
One attains immeasurable merit, and thus excels all worlds.
If there were someone who could give away mani-jewels and precious treasures,
spreading them throughout the realms of the ten directions and across immeasurable Buddha-lands.
If, for the sake of seeking the Buddha’s bodhi,
one were to give gifts to the Kings of Dharma for immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet if another person were to hear even a single phrase concerning this wondrous realm— [the latter would have generated far greater merit].
Having heard this, one who can further believe it surpasses the merit of giving immeasurably.
If there is a person of wisdom who upholds the unsurpassed precepts,
their actions of body, speech, and mind being pure, they naturally and constantly maintain them.
For the sake of seeking the Buddha’s Bodhi, throughout such immeasurable kalpas,
the merit obtained by that person is inconceivable.
Furthermore, if there is someone who hears even a single phrase regarding this wondrous realm, [their merit shall likewise be beyond measure].
Having heard this, one can further believe it; its merit exceeds that of the precepts by immeasurable degrees.
If a person enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they burn away the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms and cross to the other shore beyond the heavens;
yet, without the skillful means (*upāya*) of awakening, [this alone is insufficient].
If there is another person who hears even a single phrase concerning this wondrous realm,
and having heard it, is further able to believe it, their merit shall surpass that of dhyāna by immeasurable degrees.
A person lacking wisdom may practice renunciation, yet they will obtain only the retribution of wealth and nobility.
Those who practice and uphold the precepts will be reborn among humans and devas.
To cultivate and sever all obstacles, wisdom is indispensable;
for it is through wisdom that the afflictive obscurations are removed, and likewise, the cognitive obscurations are eliminated.
Hearing the Dharma is the cause of wisdom; therefore, hearing the Dharma is supreme.
How much more so when, having heard the Dharma, one is further able to give rise to faith.
These fourteen verses should be understood as being briefly explained by the [following] eleven verses.
The verse says:
The body and that which it transforms, merit and the accomplishment of meaning—
these four kinds of dharmas are shown to be the exclusive domain of the Tathāgata.
The wise person has faith that [the Dharma] exists, And faith that it will ultimately be attained;
By virtue of faith in all merits, They swiftly realize the unsurpassed path.
Reaching the ultimate further shore, They abide in the dwelling place of the Tathāgata.
Faith exists in that realm, which is beyond the reach of thought.
We may attain it; such are its merits. One should possess profound faith and supreme wisdom, as well as desire, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration.
Cultivating virtues such as wisdom and the unsurpassed bodhicitta,
these are always manifest before them; because they are always manifest,
they are called non-retrogressive sons of the Buddha, possessing the pure virtues of the further shore.
Ultimately they are able to achieve accomplishment.
These five perfections are meritorious qualities because they do not differentiate among the three [spheres], and because they are ultimate and pure.
Since they are free from the phenomena of antidotes, giving is solely the merit of giving.
Observing the precepts is solely the practice of ethical discipline; the other two perfections are practiced as follows:
patience and meditative concentration, while diligence pervades all stages.
The factors to be remedied by these, such as stinginess and so forth, are termed the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The false conceptualization of these three phenomena is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
To distance oneself from all such obscurations, there is no superior cause other than true, wondrous wisdom; therefore, Prajñā is supreme.
The root of that wisdom is what is called the wisdom born of hearing;
since wisdom is produced through the wisdom of hearing, hearing is therefore supreme.
Furthermore, from this point onward, the meaning of what was previously stated is clarified.
Based on what phenomena is it spoken?
Based on what meanings is it spoken?
Based on what characteristics is it spoken?
First, based on those teachings, two verses are spoken:
"This Dharma which I have taught here Is for the purification of one's own mind;
It relies upon the instructions of all Tathāgatas And accords with the Sūtras."
If there are wise people who, upon hearing this, are able to believe and accept it,
then what I have here taught is also intended to encompass them.
From this point forward, following that meaning, two verses are spoken:
Relying on lamps, lightning, mani-jewels, The sun, the moon, and other such lights,
All who possess eyes Are able to see their respective objects.
Relying on the light of the Buddha-dharma, Those with the eye of wisdom are able to see.
Because this Dharma possesses such benefits, I have taught this Dharma.
From here on, following its characteristics, two verses are spoken:
"If all that is spoken contains meaning and consists of phrases of the Dharma..."
It enables practitioners to leave the three realms far behind and reveals the dharma of tranquility—the most supreme and unsurpassed path.
The Buddha has declared this to be the true scripture; all others are inverted teachings.
From here on, based upon the skillful means of protecting the Dharma, seven verses are spoken:
Although one may explain the meaning of the words of the Dharma, The afflictions of the three realms remain;
Ignorance shrouds the eye of wisdom, And one is entangled by the stains of craving and the like.
Furthermore, regarding those who take even a small portion of the Buddha’s teachings to explain them well through worldly treatises—
even such [teachings] are worthy of acceptance;
how much more so the words of the Tathāgatas, who are far removed from the stains of affliction?
The sūtras spoken by those of untainted wisdom,
apart from the Buddhas, possess no superior wisdom within all the worlds for one who knows the Dharma as it truly is.
The Tathāgata has taught the definitive meaning, which is inconceivable;
those who attempt to conceptualize it slander the Dharma, for they do not understand the Buddha’s intention.
Such wrong reflections both slander the Noble Ones and destroy the Dharma.
Because of the false views and conceptualizations of those deluded by afflictions,
one should not cling to the defiled dharmas of wrong views;
for just as a clean cloth cannot be dyed when it is already stained with grease.
From here on, three verses are spoken concerning the slander of the True Dharma:

The foolish do not believe in the pure dharmas; Holding wrong views and arrogance, they possess the karmic obstructions of having slandered the Dharma in the past, And they cling to the provisional meaning without understanding it.
Devoted to making offerings and showing reverence, they see only false teachings;
they distance themselves from virtuous friends and draw near to those who slander the Dharma,
delighting in attachment to the Hīnayāna.
Such beings as these do not believe in the Mahāyāna, and therefore slander the teachings of the Buddhas.
From this point onward, six verses are spoken regarding the attainment of evil retributions due to slandering the True Dharma:
"The wise person should not fear enemies, snakes, fire, or poison;"
Indra’s thunderbolts, swords, staves, and various evil beasts such as lions,
tigers, and wolves— these can only sever one's life;
they cannot cause a person to enter the terrifying Avīci Hell.
One should fear slandering the profound Dharma, as well as those who are spiritual friends to the Dharma;
this will certainly cause one to enter the terrifying Avīci Hell.
Even if one associates with evil friends, or with an evil mind sheds the blood of a Buddha, [the consequences are most grave].
Even for one who has killed their father and mother, severed the lives of noble ones,
disrupted the harmony of the Saṃgha, and severed all roots of goodness—
by fixing their mindfulness upon the True Dharma, they can attain liberation from that state.
Furthermore, if there are others who slander the most profound Dharma,
those people shall not attain liberation for immeasurable kalpas.
From this point onward, two verses are spoken based on generating a heart of reverence toward the Dharma-preacher who expounds the teaching:
If there are people who cause sentient beings to study and believe in such a Dharma as this,
they are my parents and they are also my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Those people are wise, for after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, they...
To turn back false views and perversions, and cause [beings] to enter the right path.
From this point onward, in order to dedicate the merit obtained from preaching the Dharma according to that [teaching], three verses are spoken:
The pure nature of the Three Jewels, The qualities and activities of enlightenment.
I have briefly explained these seven kinds, which are in accord with the Buddha’s sutras.
By virtue of these merits, may I, at the time of death,
behold Amitāyus Buddha, whose body possesses boundless merit.
Having seen that Buddha, may I and other believers obtain the stainless eye and attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
From this point onward, the meaning of the verses is explained in brief.
The verse says:
Based on what phenomena is it taught?
Based on what meanings is it taught?
By what characteristics are they taught?
They are taught according to those phenomena, taught according to those meanings, and taught according to those characteristics.
All those phenomena are manifested through these six verses.
The skillful means for protecting oneself are explained by seven verses;
because the slandering of the True Dharma is clarified, there are three verses.
Six verses demonstrate its causes, while two verses provide the actual illustration.
Toward those who preach the Dharma, one should give rise to deep respect and reverence;
when the great assembly hears and accepts it with patience, they shall attain that Great Bodhi.
Briefly explained are these three kinds of dharmas, which manifest their karmic fruition.
